en: A Brief Introduction to the *Sūyu* (Explanatory Discourses) of the Chan Forest. That the Chan Forest possesses *sūyu* is neither a prescription of the Buddha nor a regulation of the Patriarchs.

However, since the arrival of the Sangha in this land, in order to lead all sentient beings back to the ocean of the Buddhas, there has necessarily been a reliance upon these [discourses] to manifest matters and express sentiments.

Commentary: Thus, the utility of the *shu* (commentary) has long been established. During the Tang and Song dynasties, this office was particularly esteemed within the monastic communities (*conglin*);
none were selected for it who were not preeminent in both talent and learning. Since the Ming dynasty, however, those among the clergy truly capable of this office have been rare;
instead, people merely follow established conventions and employ stale, clichéd language to offer perfunctory responses. When I formerly resided among the assembly...
Whenever I have held this office, I have suffered from the lack of precedents upon which to rely; thus, I have mostly improvised in my responses.

As these accumulated over time, I was unaware that they had formed a volume. Those with a penchant for the curious mistakenly valued them and transcribed them for circulation—this has been the case for over thirty years.
Recently, I saw that Mr. Yū Shidoku has had them carved into printing blocks at Wulin, and [the work] has reached Quannan.

The various virtuous friends have likewise continued the work from where it was left unfinished, completing it. They did so because they believed that although the matter may seem minor, its utility is truly indispensable;
and although the phrasing may be crude, the meaning can still be conveyed. This is the intention behind these gentlemen’s efforts to circulate the work.
In any great forest there must be extraordinary and eminent men; they open their mouths and pearls and gems fall forth, they wield their brushes and wind and clouds are formed.
Yet what further need is there for this? I have merely inscribed a few words to serve as an introduction to its beginning.
Shiguduzhuren (Master of the Stone Drums), Shi Yuanxian,

**Prayers for Longevity on the Emperor’s Birthday** *The Comprehensive Record of the Imperial Birthdays: On the Flowing and Obstruction of the Rites* states:

In the second year of the Shiguang era of Emperor Taizu of Northern Wei, during the anniversary of his birth, an edict was issued to establish a ritual arena (*daochang*) for prayers for longevity at Buddhist temples. (Note: This marks the beginning of the ritual arena for the Emperor’s birthday. **Prayers**
The *Shiji*, "Annals of Emperor Wen," states: "The sacrificial officials offer prayers for *li*. The commentary notes: Ru Chun says that *li* means "blessing" (*fu*).
The *Jia Yi Zhuan* states: "He received the *li* while seated in the Xuan Chamber. Su Yin says the pronunciation is *xi*, meaning "blessing" (*fu*).
I humbly submit that as the celestial signs descend from the Nine Heavens, all gaze upon the auspicious brilliance of the Sun of Shun;
as the Great Earth is governed by the Golden Wheel, all celebrate the vast majesty of the Heaven of Yao. Unable to extend our congratulations in person, we dare not delay our shouts of "Long Live!

We, [Name] and others, reflect that we were born into this prosperous age and have taken refuge in the Empty Gate. Clad in black robes and subsisting on vegetarian fare, even a drop of water is moistened by the Sage’s bounty. Dwelling among the crags...

Dwelling in caves, every inch of soil has been covered by the grace of Heaven. At this auspicious moment of beholding the flowing rainbows, my joy increases like that of a sparrow leaping for delight.

Hastening like clouds toward the sacred temple, we chant the secret scriptures with the resonance of thunder, briefly manifesting our sincerity with offerings of pondweed and algae to look up and repay the protection of the High and the Thick.

I humbly pray that Imperial Benevolence may spread ever wider and Your Majesty’s sagely longevity remain firm. May the eight directions together ascend to the era of universal harmony and prosperity for ten thousand generations.

May there be eternal security in peace and tranquility. We pray once more that we may constantly receive the grace of Heaven and continue to be favored by its radiant light. Your ministers, though silent, are secretly known and held in your esteem;
even a single inch of soil receives your nourishment, and a mere blade of grass is bathed in your glory.

○ Regarding the "Nine Heavens" (jiǔxiáo) in Pan Yue’s poem: "I wish to entrust my person to the nine heavens. Also, in Shen Xiuwen’s poem: "I entrust my aspirations to within the nine heavens. ○ Regarding "The Elephant Chariot" (xiàngyù):

The *Yì* (Book of Changes), in the *Xià cí* (Appended Phrases), states: "Heaven displays its images; therein one sees good fortune and misfortune. The sage takes these as his model. ○ Regarding Yao and Shun:
Yao was the name of the Emperor of Tang; Shun was the name of the Emperor of Yu. ○ Regarding the Golden Wheel (*jīnlún*).
See the *Shi-yuan*. ○ "The Swallows Rejoice" (*Huai-nan zi*): "When a great mansion is completed, the swallows and sparrows rejoice together. Note: A "xia" is a large house.
The swallows and sparrows rejoice because the great house is finished and they may find security within it. ○ "Crying 'Long Live' at Mount Song" (*Former Han Shu*, Basic Annals of Emperor Wu):
"I personally ascended Mount Song. My carriage was behind me, and the officials and soldiers all heard [me] cry out, 'Ten thousand years!'"
The "Three Ages" (Sui): Three. Regarding "dwelling in crags and living in caves," the *Han Shi Waizhuan* says:
"Dwelling in crags and living in caves, one’s fame cannot be vied with by kings and lords. Regarding "an inch of land," the monk Qingshun’s poem on the Ten Bamboos says:
"In the city, an inch of land is like an inch of gold. Regarding "the flow of the rainbow," the *Shouji* says: "The mother of Shaohao was named Nüjie. She had..."
The stars were like rainbows descending in streams; moved by this, Shao Hao was born. ○ Regarding "the quail leaps," the commentary on the *Zhuangzi* states:
"To pat one's belly and leap like a quail" describes the state of leaping about in self-delight. ○ Regarding "duckweed and pondweed," the poem "Plucking Duckweed" says:
"There, I pluck duckweed on the banks of the southern ravine; there, I pluck pondweed from those stagnant pools. ○
Gao Hou’s poem on the first month says: "Thinking that heaven is so high, one dares not fail to tread with circumspection;
thinking that earth is so vast, one dares not fail to step with careful care. Regarding the "Eight Horizons" (*bāhóng*), the *Huáihuánzǐ* states:

"Beyond the Nine Provinces there are the Eight Enclosures (*bāyín*); beyond the Eight Enclosures are the Eight Horizons. This means the Eight Horizons are identical to the Eight Wilds (*bāhuáng*), referring simply to the eight directions.

On the Buddha’s Birthday (the eighth day of the fourth month), we humbly reflect that while two stalks of grain grew on each ear, it was precisely the day when the Yellow Emperor mounted the Li trigram; and as the eight calendrical leaves unfolded, we rejoice in Māyā.
On this occasion of the birth of the One Who Awakens the World, we reverently observe the customary rites and exert ourselves with exceptional sincerity and devotion.

We reflect that we, [Name] and others, dwell in a realm of the five turbidities beneath the three robes; having received the moisture from the radiance of the jade-white brow, our heads and feet find it difficult to repay;

having been illumined by the light of the golden arms, not even a drop of water or a speck of dust can express our gratitude. Now, joyfully encountering the Buddha’s birthday, we have respectfully assembled the Saṃgha to scoop up fragrant waters.
We bathe the golden body [of the Buddha]. Plucking wild celery from mountain streams, we prepare this humble offering; we chant the sacred name and recite the True Vehicle (Saddharma).
May we, through these means, pour forth our sincere, ant-like devotion to repay the protection of your vast grace.

We humbly pray that your golden body may manifest once more and the waves of Dharma flow anew, so that all ordinary beings within this Sahā world may attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), and the vessel of suffering for those in the realm of birth-and-death may be entirely extinguished.
Realizing non-arising, one sweeps away the dust and grime accumulated over kalpas and washes forth the face of one’s original nature.
Regarding "Two Stalks of Wheat": the *Biography of Zhang Kan* in the *Book of the Later Han* states that Zhang Kan served as the Governor of Yuyang.

He encouraged the people to engage in agriculture and sericulture until they attained great prosperity. The people sang this song: "The mulberry has no side branches; the wheat shows two stalks on each ear. Oh, Governor Zhang!"
In governing, music cannot be over-indulged. ○ Regarding the Yellow Emperor (Yandi) mounting the *Li* trigram, the *Wei Xiang Zhuan* states:
"The Yellow Emperor mounted the *Li*, holding the balance and presiding over summer. ○ Regarding the spreading of the eight stalks of the *míng* herb, the *Diwang Shiji* states:
"During the time of Emperor Yao, there was a herb that grew along the steps; on the first day of each month it produced one stalk, and by the middle of the month it had produced ten."
There are five stalks. From the sixteenth day onward, one stalk falls at sunset each day until the end of the month, when they are all exhausted.

If the month is short, the remaining stalk dries up without falling. ○ According to the *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*), "Māyā" means "Great Artifice" (*mahāmāyā*) in the language of Tang, or "Great Illusion.
In the Chinese version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Māyādevī replies to Sudhana, saying: "I have already attained accomplishment..."
This is the Dharma-gate of the Great Vow and Wisdom-illusion. Because she has attained this Dharma-gate, she is the mother of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
In the city of Kapilavastu in Jambudvīpa, within the palace of King Śuddhodana, she gave birth to Prince Siddhārtha from her right side.
He manifested inconceivable and sovereign supernatural powers. ○ Regarding the hexagram *Zhen* (Thunder), the *Yi Zhuan Benyi* states:
"Zhen signifies movement; its image is thunder; its correlate is the eldest son. ○ Regarding the "jade tuft" (*yuhao*), see the *Shiyuan*.
○ Regarding "from the crown to the heels," the *Mencius* says: "Mozi’s universal love extended from rubbing the crown of his head to the soles of his feet for the benefit of the world."
"To act for it. The commentary states that "fàng" (放) means "to reach" (zhì). ○ Regarding "jiān'ái" (涓埃): in Du Fu’s poem *Gazing at the Wilds*, he writes:

"I offer only my declining years in service to my many ailments; I have yet to contribute even a jot or tittle (*jiān'ái*) in return for the Sagely Court. ○ The *Saṃgha-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "In the language of Qin, it means 'multitude.
When many bhikṣus are in harmonious assembly in one place, this is called a *saṃgha*. It is like a great forest of trees."

It is called a forest. ○ Regarding "Golden Body," the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states: This refers to the Tathāgata’s golden-hued body, as it is that which is spoken through the karma of speech.
○ Regarding "Wild Leeks" (*jianqin*), the *Lüshi Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn of Master Lü) says: "The rustic man loves wild leeks and wishes to offer them to the Most Honored One.
The note explains that the "Most Honored One" is the Son of Heaven. It means that the rustic man possesses only wild leeks, which he considers delicious, and desires to bring them [to him].
"To present this to the Son of Heaven—would that be permissible? The *Qixie ji* (Records of the Harmonious) by Dongyang Yuanning states:
When Dong Zhaozhi was crossing the river, he saw an ant caught in a short reed. Zhaozhi rescued it. Later, he was imprisoned.
The ants led the swarm into their burrows like prisoners entering a dungeon; thus, Zhao escaped with his life. ○ *Hóngxiū* (Great Auspiciousness):
*Hóng* and *hóng* are interchangeable; it means "great. *Xiū* means "beauty" or "auspiciousness. ○ Regarding the "Original Face":

The *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) states that Daoming sought the Dharma from the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch asked, "Which one is the original face of Master Ming?"

On the Buddha’s Day of Enlightenment (the eighth day of the tenth month), we humbly reflect that auspicious signs have dawned with the commencement of the Shang season, and the jade palace shines brilliantly on this eighth day.

May these portents accord with the Dharma-transformation, as the practices of the Snowy Mountains reach fulfillment over three *kalpas*. We respectfully follow the pure regulations to manifest our sincere devotion. We, [Name] and others, reflect deeply upon our eternal dwelling in the darkness...
The nights are long in the city of awakening, and as time slips away, one remains lost at the ford of the stream. Beholding the morning star, one fails to awaken;

traversing the rugged and perilous path, one finds it difficult to reach the Snowy Peaks. Fortunately, the Great Awakened One has revealed the period of his attainment of enlightenment, whereby this common fool may open the path of self-renewal.
We respectfully prepare the *īpū* offering and reverently unroll the chapters of the *bā-ye* [Palm-leaf] scriptures, hoping to exhaust our humble sincerity and offer a small recompense.

Under your compassionate protection, we humbly pray that the Dharma conch shall forever resound and the snares of Māra remain hidden. May the river of meditation deepen with waves in ten thousand streams, and the tree of enlightenment flourish with splendor throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes.
May all together take refuge in the land of awakening and jointly propagate the profound Way.

○ Regarding "The Shang calendar was based on the first month of winter" (商正左), the commentary states: The Xia calendar established the eleventh month as the start of the year; the Shang established the twelfth month; and the Zhou established the first month.
○ The *Xuanyu* (Book of the Mysterious Universe) quotes the "Canon of Shun" (*Shundian*): "With the *xuánjī* and *yùhéng*, he aligned the seven celestial offices.

The commentary states: *Xuán* refers to beautiful jade. It rotates while the *héng* remains level. An instrument made of jade for the *jī* and *héng* is called the *hùntiānyí* (spherical armillary sphere). ○ *Sānzhī* (Three Kalpas).
The *Shiyuan* states: "Saṃkhyeya" means "immeasurable. This refers to the World-Honored One’s cultivation of practice over three *asaṃkhyeyas*.
From the initial arousal of the mind at the stage of the ten faiths until reaching the first name of the world is called the first *asaṃkhyeya*.
From the path of seeing until the end of the seventh bhūmi is called the second *asaṃkhyeya*. From the eighth bhūmi until the path of liberation is called the third.
*Saṃgha-koṭi*. Outside of these three *koṭis*, one may attain Buddhahood. *Qinggui* (Pure Rules):

The Great Wisdom Master Hai of Baizhang Mountain established the ritual protocols for the monastic community (*conglin*), naming them the *Qinggui*. *Renran biezhuan* (Commentary on the Gradual Transmission) states:
It describes the manner of lingering or delaying; it also carries the sense of successive transmission. "Beholding the morning star" refers to the dawn star. Cultivating practice.
The *Benqi jing* states: "The Bodhisattva knows for himself that he has already abandoned the roots of evil; lust, anger, and delusion no longer exist. Birth and death have been eliminated;
the various seeds of the five aggregates are entirely severed, with no remaining vestiges. What was to be done has been accomplished, and wisdom is fully realized."
When the morning star appeared, he attained great enlightenment; he realized the Unsurpassed, Right, and True state as the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
*Qíqū guī qù lái cí zhù*: "Qíqū" means rugged and perilous. Regarding the food offered in the *ípú* vegetarian feast, it is called *ípú zhuàn*.
During the Later Han dynasty, King Ying of Chu went to the palace gate to redeem his transgressions by offering silk. The Emperor’s decree in response stated: "The King is fond of..."
The words of Huang-Lao venerated the teachings of the Buddha; they returned the ransom money to assist in providing food for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas*.
(Note: *Upāsaka* is the same as *i-pu-se*; this means "one who dwells near," signifying that by receiving the precepts, one dwells very close to the Sangha.
According to the *Piyelimingji* (Collection of Names and Meanings of Palm Leaves): *Tāla* was formerly called *Beidu*. This...
The *tāla* tree: its shape is like that of the local *tāla* palm, straight and tall, reaching an extreme height and length of eighty or ninety feet.
Its flowers resemble yellow millet seeds. Some say that one *tāla* tree is seven *ren* high; seven feet is called one *ren*.
This tree was forty-nine feet high. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"Not far to the north of the kingdom of Kanyākubja in South India, there is a forest of tala trees extending for more than thirty li. Their leaves are long and broad, and their color is lustrous;
no country employs them for writing more than this."

On the day of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa (the fifteenth day of the second month), when the full moon—a solitary orb—reaches its peak in the eastern land of China, a season of vigorous youth and Yang energy, while in the western land of India, the region where he demonstrated the end of his transformative life, his radiance fades beneath the twin trees, our longing and reverence deepen.
We respectfully perform these Brahma-rites. We reflect that we, [Name] and others, have sunk into the ocean of illusory transformations and remain mired in ignorance.
Nirvana Heaven: Pursuing existence while clinging to non-existence, they have yet to recognize the aperture through which one returns to the Truth.
In birth and death, who can discern the source of eternal quiescence? Only our Buddha has revealed the field of Great Nirvana and acts as the true Lord of refuge for all sentient beings.
Our gratitude is such; from where could we possibly repay His virtue? On this occasion of the anniversary of His Nirvana, we specifically present these pure offerings.
Offerings. (Virtues of Following Entry) We humbly pray that the *dharma* flowers may bloom once more and the Twin Footprints of the Golden One be clearly manifested.

May the Perfect Sound be perpetually proclaimed, opening the final secret treasury of all Buddhas; may the flames of wisdom blaze anew, shattering the gates of beginningless delusion for sentient beings.
May the compassionate radiance universally illuminate the ten directions, and may the joy of the Dharma be shared by all within the nine realms.
The Dongzhen Shiyuan states: Some call it Zhendan, some Zhandan, some Zhidan, and some Zhinan;
these are all corruptions of the Sanskrit sound, all translated as "Han Land. The *Xiyuji* translates Mahācīna as "Great Han Country.
It is also said that because the sun rises from the eastern corner and its color is like vermilion (dan), it is called Zhendan or Zhendan.

These are all erroneous explanations. ○ Regarding the term *pò* (魄): that which refers to the dark body of the moon is called *pò*. "Dead *pò*" (*sǐpò*) refers to the first day of the lunar month (*shuò*).
"Living *pò*" (*shēngpò*) refers to the full moon (*wàng*). ○ The *Xīqián Shìyuàn* states: "Xīqián" refers to the land of the five Indias in India, or what is called "Western Heaven.
○ For the "Two Trees," see the *Mìngyì jí*. ○ For "filial longing" (*rúmù*), see the poem on the *táng* tree.

**Note on *Dì* (棣):** "Rú" (孺) refers to the affectionate longing of a small child for its parents. **Nirvāṇa:** *Nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term. In this [Chinese] language, it is translated as "Extinction and Deliverance" (*mièdù*).
This means that by eliminating afflictions (*kleśa*), one crosses over birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, "Nir" (*niē*) signifies non-arising, and "Vāṇa" (*pán*) signifies non-extinction;
because it is neither arising nor extinction, it is named *nirvāṇa*. **The Name and Meaning of the *Tánhuā* (Utpala Flower):** [To be continued].
The *Ji* says: This is called "Auspicious Response. The *Panniehuan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) states:
"Within Jambudvīpa there is a sovereign king of trees named Udumbara; it bears fruit but has no flowers. When the Udumbara tree bears golden flowers, a Buddha appears in the world.
The *Jinzutong zai* says: The Buddha told his great disciples, "When Kāśyapa arrives, you may..."
"Command that the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be proclaimed. At that time, Kāśyapa was at the Piṇḍola Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Beholding a supreme radiance, he immediately entered samādhi. With his pure divine eye, he perceived that the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa by the side of the Hiraṇyavatī River.
He then addressed his disciples, saying: "The Tathāgata has entered nirvāṇa! How tragic!"
Swiftly, he arrived at the space between the twin trees and wailed in sorrowful longing. The Buddha manifested his two feet from within the golden coffin.
According to the *Jiujie yaolan* (Essentials of the Nine Realms): first, the Ground of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies; second, the Ground of Joy and Bliss Arising from Seclusion.

The third is the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration; the fourth is the stage of sublime bliss born of seclusion; the fifth is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness; the sixth is the stage of the sphere of infinite space;

the seventh is the stage of the sphere of infinite consciousness; the eighth is the stage of the sphere of nothingness; and the ninth is the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding these stages, there are four meanings: namely, abode, inclusion, cultivation, and governance.
The Liturgy for Recitation on the Day of Nirvana (The Venerable Leader Steps Forward and Announces):

We reverently hear that the Benevolent One responded to the world, attaining the truth through silent stillness. He dwells as the Honored One throughout the thousand worlds, and treats the four classes of living beings as his children.

His form manifests according to the needs of things, yet it is fundamentally identical to the body beyond signs; his teachings arise in accordance with the capacities of beings, yet they are no different from the wordless.

The Way of the Buddha: since the Wheel of Dharma first turned, the traces of his transformation have flourished ever more. When the "half-letters" were first expounded, he was tireless in striking away the ignorance of the deluded;

The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states regarding the four conditions: [text follows].
First is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) acting as the cause and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) acting as the condition.

For example, when the eye faculty encounters a visual object, consciousness arises accordingly; the same applies to the other faculties. This is called the causal condition. Second is the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

This refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) arising in immediate succession and continuity. This is called the sequential condition. Third is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This refers to the fact that mental states and their concomitants arise by depending on conditions; yet these very conditions are themselves what the mind takes as its objects of cognition.

This is called the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition). The fourth is the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition). This refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which are capable of illuminating objects and giving rise to consciousness.

Because they possess this superior functional power and do not create obstacles when various phenomena arise, they are called the dominant condition. [Signature/Note]: "Cun-gong" (A Small Measure of Merit) — Du Fu.

On behalf of the deceased [Name], the Sangha has performed the two fascicles of the *Lianghuang Chanfa* (Repentance Ritual of Emperor Liang). Relying upon this sublime scripture, we exhaust our humble sincerity.

As the merit of these two fascicles is completed, we briefly offer this dedication of merit. We humbly pray that the deceased’s awakened mind may never grow dim and their power of aspiration ever expand;
that they may increase the two adornments to universally benefit both enemies and kin, and fulfill the two practices so that all sentient beings within the realms of existence may find sustenance.
[The two adornments are explained above. Regarding the second [section], the *Huayan jing shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states: "First, all practices are accomplished instantaneously;
second, all practices are accomplished universally; third, [they are] rolled up..."

I, [Name], reflect deeply that I have indulged my perverse thoughts and recklessly given rise to deluded karma. Consequently, I have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts or sunk into the hells like an echo responding to a sound;
I dwell among humans or enter the animal realm like a shadow following a form. My suffering is acute yet there is no one to whom I can cry out;

when conditions converge, there is no way to escape. Therefore, on this very day, I rely upon the Sangha to perform, on behalf of the deceased [Name], the Threefold Repentance of the Liang Emperor’s Dharma.
I now rely upon this wondrous scripture to exhaust my humble sincerity. As the merit of these three scrolls is completed, I briefly offer this dedication of merit.

I humbly pray that [Name] may uproot the three poisons and tear asunder the net of the three karmas; that by relying on the purity of both self and others, they may forever cast aside the anxieties of calamity and adversity;
and that by forgetting both self and other, they may eternally eliminate the suffering of obstacles.
I repeatedly contemplate that the karmic power of sentient beings such as [Name] is inexhaustible, and the fire-wheels of hell blaze with particular intensity.

Were it not for the Buddhas extending their radiance, how could this scorching affliction be suddenly extinguished? Were it not for a single thought of repentance, by what means could one be suddenly drenched in purity?

It is cool. Thus, on this very day, we rely upon the Sangha to perform, on behalf of the deceased [Name], the fourth fascicle of the *Lianghuang Chanchan Fa* (The Ritual of Repentance of Emperor Liang).

By means of this sublime scripture, we exhaust our humble sincerity. As the merit of the four fascicles is completed, we briefly offer this dedication of merit. We humbly pray that the flames of the city of fire may be extinguished and the blades of the sword-tree forest shattered.
May the Golden Land be fully revealed, where gentle breezes stir the resonance of the Jewel Forest, and the Iron Ring Mountains shall no longer appear. May there be sweet dew...
Dew flows with the ripples of the emerald pond.
For five volumes, I have vainly given rise to the three poisons and indulged the six sense faculties; thus, the sentiments of provocation have become entangled and remain unreleased.
The karma of resentment increases ever further without ceasing; by this, the six realms of existence circulate, and by this, one sinks and falls into the three miserable paths.
Therefore, on this very day, [the living] rely upon the Sangha to perform, on behalf of the deceased [Name], the fifth fascicle of the Liang Emperor’s Repentance Method.
Relying upon this wondrous scripture, I exhaust my humble sincerity. As the merit of these five fascicles is completed, I briefly offer this dedication.
I humbly pray that [Name] may forget both giving and reward, benefiting both self and others; that with joy like that of the First Ground, they may travel together in the Heaven of Non-contention;
and that with unimpededness like the great void, they may enter together the realm of True Emptiness.

Six volumes of earnest contemplation: I, [Name], through greed, anger, and delusion, have moved my body, speech, and mind. As one gives forth, so shall one receive; the momentum of this reciprocity is inevitable.
Morning after morning and evening after evening, it remains thus. How can the cycle of retribution ever end? Even for a single matter, the consequences persist until the very end.

The resentment of the body binds a grievance for ten thousand generations in a single moment. Therefore, on this very day, [the living] rely upon the monks (on behalf of the deceased, [Name]) to perform the sixth fascicle of the *Lianghuang Chanchan Fa*.
By means of this wondrous scripture, they exhaust their humble sincerity; as the merit of the six fascicles is completed, they briefly offer this dedication.
We prostrate with the hope that [Name]'s resentments may dissipate like mist and their doubts melt like ice, so that the Gate of Non-duality may be made level and open.
Nevertheless, they enter together; the path returning to the origin is vast and traversed by all alike.
"What goes out from you must return to you" (孟子, Book 7).

I, [Name], reflect deeply that having joyfully encountered this era of the Great Teaching, I cherish the sacred grace of the Sages. It is no mere coincidence that we now practice together through the power of the multitude;

it is truly the fulfillment of my original aspiration to give rise to vast vows for the sake of the inexhaustible. Moved by the kindness of Heaven, I contemplate how to repay it; burdened by the support of the Immortals’ power, I give rise to profound reverence.
Therefore, on this very day, I rely upon the Sangha to perform, on behalf of the deceased [Name], the seventh fascicle of the Liang Emperor’s Repentance Rite (*Lianghuang Chanfa*).
Relying upon this wondrous scripture, I exhaust my humble sincerity; as the merit of these seven fascicles is completed, I briefly offer this dedication.

I prostrate with the wish that [I, so-and-so] may not render this singular auspicious occasion in vain, but be worthy of repaying the grace of the Triple Gem. May I awaken to the nature of the Dharma-realm as fundamentally perfect, forever extinguishing the outflows of the seven afflictions;
may I enter the adamantine mind without decay, and suddenly fulfill the merit of the seven stages of enlightenment.
The *Qiqing qunshu shisu* states: "The seven emotions are joy, anger, love, suffering, grief, hatred, and desire.
The *Qijue fajie cidi* says: 1. The awakening factor of investigation of dharmas; 2. The awakening factor of energy; 3. The awakening factor of joy; 4.
The awakening factor of tranquility; 5. The awakening factor of equanimity; 6. The awakening factor of concentration; 7. The awakening factor of mindfulness.

I have constantly and earnestly contemplated that those dwelling as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) in such-and-such places—whether they belong to the ranks of *asuras* or *māras*—all partake in the merit of being shielded and protected;
and whether they belong to the human realm or the class of *nāgas* and spirits, all alike receive the virtue of being molded and perfected. Had it not been for this taking refuge in the Buddha...

With sincere devotion, how can I fully manifest my diligent efforts to repay this kindness? Therefore, on this very day, I rely upon the Sangha (on behalf of the deceased, [Name]) to perform the eighth fascicle of the *Liang Emperor’s Repentance Method*.
By means of this sublime scripture, I exhaust my humble sincerity; as the merit of these eight fascicles is completed, I briefly offer this dedication.

I humbly pray that [Name] may cross the ocean of karmic obstacles and emerge from the land of worldly toil; that the eight heterodoxies be simultaneously extinguished, utterly pruning away the thorny brambles that pierce the heavens;
and that the eight consciousnesses be all shattered, forever causing the empty flowers before one’s eyes to vanish.

wrong concentration; 7. wrong mindfulness; 8. wrong livelihood. ○ Regarding the Eight Consciousnesses, the *Zongjing lu* states:
1. visual consciousness; 2. auditory consciousness; 3. olfactory consciousness; 4. gustatory consciousness; 5. tactile consciousness; 6. mental consciousness.

I am reluctant to delay further. Since all conditioned things are not enduring, how could one permit greed or attachment?

Relying upon this assembly who have exerted their strength and endured labor, we have successfully completed the means for cultivating causes and eliciting results. Therefore, on this very day, I rely upon the Sangha to perform, on behalf of the deceased [Name], the ninth fascicle of the Liang Emperor’s Repentance Method (*Lianghuang Chanchan*).
By means of this sublime scripture, I exhaust my humble sincerity; as the work of the nine fascicles is complete, I briefly offer this dedication of merit.

I humbly pray that [Name] may cast off the net of outflows and emerge from the pit of impermanence; that the nine fetters may be instantly extinguished as they ascend directly to the realm of liberation;
and that, unimpeded by the nine realms, they may straightway attain the field of Bodhi.

Regarding the nine fetters (*navasaṃyojana*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: first, the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*); second, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); third, the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*); fourth, the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*);

fifth, the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); sixth, the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*); seventh, the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*); eighth, the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*); and ninth, the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
The nine realms are seen above.

Ten volumes of constant recitation—[for the sake of] (Name)—enduring suffering, laying bare one’s sincerity, and braving toil to cultivate repentance. How could the accumulation of these roots of goodness be restricted to a single [realm]?
A person’s great vows, once extended, must surely reach far across the six realms of existence. Furthermore, I harbor deep fears that the flow of the Dharma’s transformation may be severed;

how then could I dare not be sincere in this entrustment? Therefore, on this very day, I rely upon the Sangha to perform the tenth fascicle of the *Liang Emperor’s Repentance Ritual* for the sake of the deceased [Name].
By means of this sublime scripture, I exhaust my humble sincerity; as the merit of the ten fascicles is completed, I offer this small tribute.
Dedication. We humbly pray that [Name] may cultivate the practice of ultimate realization and attain the merit of perfection;
that the ten titles may all be manifested to achieve the unsurpassed, wondrous fruit, and that the ten bodies may appear together to extensively deliver boundless sentient beings.

○ See the *Jianyao-lan* (Essential Compendium) for the ten titles. ○ Regarding the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Huayan jiaomen zhi zhang* (Manual of the Avataṃsaka Teaching Gate) states:
The ten bodies of the Tathāgata are: first, the Bodhi-body; second, the Vow-body; third, the Transformation-body; fourth, the Sustaining-power body;
fifth, the Body adorned with the primary and secondary marks; sixth, the Majestic-power body; seventh, the Mind-born body; eighth, the Merit-body; ninth, the Dharma-body; tenth, [the Wisdom-body].
The Body of Wisdom.
*Kōshō of the Zenrin Sogo*, Volume One;
*Kōshō of the Zenrin Sogo*, Volume Two.
In this Gate of Averting Calamities, the Prayer for Rain in Spring:
The Great Movement is now turning back, reaching the season of generative vitality; yet, as the spring rains have not yet fallen, the merit of planting and cultivation cannot be realized.
We await only the dawn of renewal; how could we dare forget our earnest prayers?

We, [Name] and others, reflect that while we have diligently labored at the eastern fields and applied our wits to the western harvests, we have now encountered the time governed by the Green Emperor, only for the drought-demon to suddenly unleash its tyranny.

The green wheat by the swelling waves is withered by disease, and the yellow seedlings emerging from the water are ruined and parched. If the spring sowing is thus, what hope remains for the autumn harvest?
We respectfully cultivate the Brahma-scriptures to earnestly invoke Your Holy Compassion. (Entering the Buddhist service:
We humbly pray that the Wind Deity will manifest his spiritual power and the Rain Deity will perform his duty, bestowing moisture that drenches the heavens, pouring forth and flowing in abundance.
May the sounds of joy replace those of distress; may the sorrowful find delight and the sick be healed.
The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) states: "We wait for our sovereign; when the sovereign comes, we shall revive. The commentary explains that "revive" (*su*) means to return to life.
The commentary on the *Shangshu* regarding "Eastern labor and Western harvest" explains: "Eastern labor" refers to the spring months, when the annual labors of the year first arise;
it denotes the tasks that ought to be initiated. "Western harvest" refers to the autumn months, the time when things reach fruition; it denotes that which ought to be brought to completion.

This is a matter of fact. ○ Regarding the Green Emperor (Qingdi), see the preceding section. ○ Regarding the poem "Yunhan" concerning the drought-demon (Hanzhab): "The drought has become exceedingly great;
the mountains and rivers are parched, and the drought-demon (hanzhab) inflicts its cruelty. Note: The hanzhab is the deity of drought.

○ Regarding the Wind Earl (Fengbo) and Rain Master (Yushi), the *Fengsu tong* states: "According to the *Zhouli*, one sacrifices to the Wind Master with a willow torch. The Wind Master is the constellation Jishi."
The winnowing basket (*ji*) presides over winnowing and can bring forth wind. Furthermore, one sacrifices with burning wood (*yǒu liáo*) to the Rain Master (*yǔ shī*).
The Rain Master is the constellation *Bi*. As the *Shijing* says: "When the moon leaves *Bi*, it causes torrents to pour down. (Commentary: "Leaving" refers to the place where the moon lodges.
*Bi* is the name of a constellation. When the moon leaves *Bi*, it is a sign that rain is imminent. ○ "Péirán" (Pouring down): the commentary on Mencius states this means heavy rain.

Appearance. ○ "Yangran" (洋然) refers to an appearance of grandeur and abundance. ○ Regarding the expressions "the sorrowful find joy" and "the sick recover," see Su Shi’s *Record of the Pavilion for Joyful Rain*.
Summer Prayer for Rain.
The sun blazes with crimson light; who can ward off the agony of the flowing gold? The fields are parched and the green crops wither; when will there be the hope of cooking jade-like grain?

We look upward to pray at the Lion Terrace, wishing that you would have compassion for our ant-like sincerity. We, [Name] and others, reflect that we live in humble thatched huts and know the hardships of sowing and reaping.
We joyfully exerted all our strength in the spring plowing, only to be suddenly struck with alarm by the summer drought. The ears of grain, once lush and flourishing, are now gradually...
The yellow grain of the wilds of Bin is withered; the millet there is falling away and will soon wither on the white plains of Zhou.
It has reached its ultimate limit. How bitter it is! I respectfully lead the common people to take special refuge in the Triple Gem. (Enter for the Buddhist rite.

We pray that you shall rouse the slumbering dragon and manifest the majesty of thunder and lightning. Let your bounty descend copiously and flow forth abundantly, extinguishing the flames of the red furnace and emerging...
[The character] "to act. Entering and breathing, one brings back the harmony of the vast green fields.
*Liujin* (Melting Gold): Zhuangzi says, "In a great drought, metal and stone melt, and the earthen mountains wither. *Cuiyu* (Cooking Jade):
The *Zhan Guo Ce* says, when Su Qin reached the state of Chu, he was granted an audience with the King after three days. He said, "The food in the state of Chu is expensive."

Regarding jade: firewood is more precious than cinnamon. Now, this humble messenger is made to eat jade and cook with cinnamon. From the poem by Yang Shigu: "Lord Zhang is pressed for fuel, cooking jade;
he rents a house and finds only an empty hearth. [The character] *yǐ* (蟻) appears above. Regarding the phrase "the grain stalks are lush":
from the *Shengmin* (The People) ode of the *Beishan* (Bin) fields, it says, "The grain stalks are lush. The commentary states: "Lush" refers to the beauty of the sprouts.

[This refers to] appearance. It is also said: "He cleared away the luxuriant grasses and sowed the yellow, flourishing grains. The commentary states that "yellow, flourishing grains" refers to auspicious cereals.

Furthermore, the preface to the *Feng* (Wind) section of the *Shi Jing* (Book of Odes) notes: "Bin was the name of a state. It was located north of Mount Qi in the region of Yongzhou as defined in the *Yu Gong* (Tributes of Yu), within the wilds of the high plains and marshes.
Gouliu was able to restore and cultivate the legacy of Hou Ji; thus the people became wealthy and prosperous, and they subsequently examined the nature of the land."
"It would be appropriate to establish the state in the valley of Bīn. "The millet grows tall and lush; the plain of Zhōu is white.

(From the *Shī* [Classic of Poetry], "Millet in Separation" [Shǔlí]; "lush" means hanging down in appearance). The *Shī* [Classic of Poetry], "The Origin of Zhōu" [Mián] says: "The plain of Zhōu is rich and fertile. (Commentary: Zhōu is the name of a place).

To the south of Mount Qi, a broad and level plain is called an *yuan*. "Wu-wu" describes a beautiful, lush, and fertile appearance. Regarding the hibernation of the *jiao* and dragon, the *Yi Zhuan* (Commentary on the Appended Phrases) states:
"The hibernation of dragons and snakes is for the purpose of preserving their bodies. Regarding the majesty of thunder and lightning, Du Fu’s poem says:
"Bees and wasps ultimately harbor venom; thunder and lightning can strike with awe-inspiring power. "Pai-ran" and "yang-ran" describe a state of overflowing abundance and vastness.
See above. ○ Regarding "extinguishing by smothering," the *Shu Jing* (Book of Documents), in the "Pan Geng" chapter, says: "It is like a fire blazing across the wilds;
it cannot be approached from near, yet it may still be extinguished by smothering. ○ Regarding "going out one works, coming in one rests," see above.

In praying for rain this autumn, farmers look toward a bountiful harvest with joy as the autumn moon approaches; yet, fearing the calamity of the drought-demon, their anxiety is as great as treading upon spring ice.

Bowing low, we exhaust our humble sincerity; looking upward, we pray for Your Sacred Compassion. We, [Name] and others, reflect that while we seek our livelihood upon the fields of Yu, we live amidst the plains of Zhou.
I reckon: how could I have expected that at this time of harvest, such scorching heat would still prevail?

The clouds hang thick, yet the wind thins them; the sun shines brilliantly, yet the rain does not arrive. Thus, planting rice has turned into painting cakes, and for curing hunger, how can one steam sand?
Therefore, I call upon the Buddha, the Awakened King, and respectfully present these Buddhist rites. (Enter for the Buddhist rites) I pray that you will pour forth the spring of nectar.

The waters of Great Compassion were poured forth; they rose up like oil and descended in torrents. Silver bamboos sprang up and spread their moistening dew, bringing joy to the plowmen and delight to the sorrowful.
Thus was the auspicious omen of a golden year of abundance brewed and matured.
○ "The drought-demon appears" (from the *Shangshu*). ○ Regarding the passage in the *Shujing* addressed to Junya:
"The anxiety of my heart is as if treading upon a tiger's tail or wading across spring ice. The commentary states: "It is like wading across spring ice, fearing one might sink.

○ Regarding "Yu tilled the land" (from the *Mao Shi*): "Truly, that Southern Mountain was tilled by Yu. The commentary states: "Tilled (*dian*) means cultivated. ○ Regarding "The plain of Zhou" (*Zhouyuan*).
See above. ○ Regarding "cloud-screens" (*yún píng*): The *Hòuyǔ* of the *Chūcí* says: "The wrath of the Wind Earl—by whom was it sent?
Cloud-screens hang thickly, blowing [the wine] so that its flavor is diluted. ○ Regarding "the sun is bright white" (*rì gǎogǎo*): Mencius says: "The autumn sun exposes it;
how bright white it is, beyond compare! ○ Regarding "painted cakes": The *Weijì* records an edict from Emperor Ming addressed to Lu... [text fragment].
Yù said: "In selecting officials, do not choose those who merely have a reputation; it is like drawing figures on the ground to represent cakes—one cannot eat them.
Regarding "steaming sand," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one does not sever lust yet practices meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and stones in the hope of producing rice;
though it passes through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it remains nothing but hot sand. [Then the rain] flowed forth and descended in torrents.
Mencius said: "Heaven gives rise to clouds in profusion and pours down rain in abundance. *Yinzhu* (Silver Bamboo), from a poem by Li Bai: "White rain reflects against the cold mountains;
dense and tall, they resemble silver bamboo. *Zhannru* (Moistening), from a poem by Luoyan: "Wind and clouds gather together; dew and rain each moisten all things.
Regarding *yunnang* (fermentation/steeping), the *Huainanzi Benjing* says: "To measure and pour out [the essence]."
The myriad differences are vast and manifold; through their mutual interaction and incubation, they bring all things to fruition and nurture the multitude of living beings.

"To extinguish by striking" (*pūmiè*); see above. "Lù Gāo"; in the twenty-first year of Duke Āi of Lù, he entered into an alliance with the Marquis of Qí.
Regarding the "Gu": The people of Qi reproached him with a prostration and sang this song: "The gao of the men of Lu has lasted for years; it does not cause me to leap high.
(The phrase "fang cun xin" [the square-inch heart] appears above. Regarding "zhu zi": The *Liji* states, "To divide a state as if it were a *zi* or a *zhu*.
The commentary notes that eight *liang* make one *zi-zhu*. It refers to the weight of ten grains of millet on a scale. Regarding "Xuamming": [The term for the Dark Spirit.]
The planet Mars appears simultaneously with those mentioned above;

the threat of pestilence and epidemics spreading like the wind is truly urgent, causing great anxiety for the people of Fen-yu. With sincere devotion, I venture to entrust this proclamation to the piety of the bhikṣus.
With profound reverence, we pray before the majestic Great Awakened One; with utmost humility, we cultivate our service with sincere devotion.

We reflect that none among us are anything other than common mortals with horizontal eyes—who among us is a true man of self-restraint? Recently, observing the calamities of the six portents, we truly see the distress of the masses.
We have failed to avoid transgressions and fear the reprimand of the August Heaven; having committed offenses, we find it difficult to evade [the consequences].
Increasing the transgressions recorded in the Black Register, I now seek to atone before the Lord of Plagues by offering this sincere devotion to the sacred scriptures.

(Entering the ritual) I pray that the sounds of wailing may be transformed into melodic chants, and that pestilential vapors may be converted into auspicious breezes. First, longevity; second, blessings.

Third is "Peace" (ning): we all rely upon the bestowal of the *Ji Chou* (The Nine Divisions of the Great Plan), where ten form a "league" (*lian*), five form a "neighborhood" (*bi*), and four form a "clan" (*zu*), living in mutual security within the leisurely ease of the Zhou dynasty's well-field system.
*Fenyu*: Both [the characters for] *bīchū* (bhikṣu) appear above. Regarding "small mind," the *Daming* (Great Brightness) says: "This King Wen was small-minded and cautious (*xiāoxīn yìyì*).
The commentary notes that *yìyì* means "reverent. Regarding "people with horizontal eyes," the *Zhuangzi* says: [The people of the North Sea have eyes on their foreheads.]
Yuancheng Feng said: "Does the Master have no concern for those people with horizontal eyes? In the *Shenjian* (Examination of the Self), the *Yixun* states:

"When occupying a superior position, one must be capable of clarity; when acting as a subordinate, one must be capable of loyalty. In dealing with others, do not seek perfection; in examining oneself, act as if one has not yet reached it.

Regarding the "Six Calamities" (*liuzhen*), the *Kongguang Zhuan* says: "As for the manifestation of the six calamities," [Master] Shigu’s commentary states: "Liuzhen. (The term *liuzhen* refers to the six types of portents or disturbances.)
It is an evil vapor; its pronunciation is *lì*. ○ "To have few transgressions" has not yet been seen in the *Xianwen* [of the Analects].
○ The "Fu on the Imperial Vault of Heaven for a Widow" says: "I look up to the Imperial Vault of Heaven and sigh. The commentary states this refers to Heaven.
○ "To commit calamity is difficult to evade" is seen in the *Shangshu*, Taijia. ○ The *Heibo Zhilun* says: "The names of good and evil karma are 'black' and 'white. Various sutras and treatises...
It is said that King Yama records the good and evil karma of the deceased. Those with virtuous karma are inscribed on golden tablets;
those with evil karma are recorded in iron registers. Regarding longevity and blessings, see the passage above. Concerning the "lian" (league) and "bi" (neighboring group), the *Zhou Li* states:
"Ten states constitute a league (*lian*), which has a commander. Five households form a neighborhood (*bi*), and four *li* (wards) form a clan (*zu*)."

My family has been afflicted by pestilence and epidemics, causing us suffering beyond measure. Overwhelmed by this pressing personal anxiety, I maintain a sense of solemn caution and dread within my heart, lest I incur the regret of biting my own heels.
Looking up, I bring this before Your Azure Eyes; looking down, I exhaustively express my sincere devotion. I, [Name], reflect most earnestly that [my life] is as light as a goose feather...
My life is as fragile as the light of a firefly or a torch; my words are slight and thus bring me dishonor, and my conduct is thin and thus incurs guilt.
Failing to reflect upon one’s virtue, one does not perform even small good deeds, nor does one abandon even small evils; thus, transgression quickly takes root within one's person.

Observing that the spread of pestilence has become increasingly severe, my heart trembles with apprehension, truly fearing it will continue to spread. Thinking to prevent it before it reaches the mulberry trees, I respectfully cultivate the rites of the Buddhist scriptures, hoping thereby to be liberated.
The Registers of the Epidemic Officials. (Entering for the Buddhist service: We humbly pray that through this resonance, all shall be communicated and those with transgressions be forgiven.

May the entire family share in auspicious celebration, remaining forever at peace within the harmony of the five phases; may the four seasonal energies be constantly regulated, eternally eliminating the calamities of the six portents.

Regarding "zhā-cái" (札瘥), Du Yu’s commentary on the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "Premature death is called zhā; minor epidemics are called cái. "Vigilance and trepidation" (*jìjǐn kǒngjù*) appears in the *Zhōngyōng*.
Regarding "biting one's navel" (*shìqí*), the *Zuo Zhuan*, Year 6 of Duke Zhuang, records that the three nephews said:

"The one who destroyed the state of Deng is this man. If you do not plan for him early, later Your Majesty will bite your own navel. The commentary notes that this is like biting one's own belly-navel, serving as a metaphor for a desperate situation.
It is unattainable. ○ Regarding "a goose’s down" (*hong-mao*): the *Biography of Sima Qian* states, "All people must inevitably die;

yet death may be as heavy as Mount Tai, or it may be as light as a goose’s down. ○ "To bring calamity upon oneself" (*su-li-yu-gong*). ○ "Trembling with apprehension" (*zhan-jing*). ○ "To remove [the roof] before the mulberry tree" (*che-sang*).
○ The six types of baleful influences (*liu-li*) are all seen above.

On this day of averting the cattle plague, observing the livestock epidemics, one realizes that the plowing of the southern fields is truly superior. With the sincerity of an ant, I offer this proclamation at the western suburb for the seasonal sacrifice.
Holding fast to the thought that the labor of the humble farmer truly relies upon the Great Martial Power to accomplish its work—how could such a thing be abandoned? It is sufficient indeed.

It has been employed. Who would have thought that the pestilence of widespread death would be more severe than the distress of the "ku-sou" ox, or that the gasping of the Han capital might lead to injury?
That those who die in the imperial hall may do so without guilt—this I respectfully entrust to the dark-clad monks to specially entreat Your Imperial Compassion.

(Enter for the ritual) We humbly pray that You will extend the grace of the covering heavens and bestow upon these beings the nature of the supporting earth, so that they shall suffer neither calamity nor harm. Even if...

His spirit dwelt amidst the grasses and wilds, perhaps even in his place of rest; he let his will roam beneath the peach grove so that [the crops] might flourish and grow strong, assisting me in my plowing and weeding.
○ South Fields ○ Ant-like Sincerity ○ The Sacrifice of the Western Suburb ○ The prevalence of pestilence and famine is seen as above. ○ The *Huo* (calamity).
Regarding the distress over the ox, Mencius said: "King Xuan of Qi was sitting in his hall when a man passed by the lower part of the hall leading an ox.
The King saw him and asked, 'Where is this ox being taken? The man replied, 'It is to be used for the blood-consecration of the bells. The King said, 'Release it!
I cannot bear to see its quivering, terrified form as it goes to its death like one who is innocent. The man replied, 'If that is so, then let the rite be abandoned.'"

Regarding the "sacrificing a sheep for the bell": [The Duke of She] asked, "How can it be discarded? and had a sheep substituted for it. As for the "heaving sigh of the capital of Han," this refers to Ceng Ji of the Former Han.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan, he served as Chancellor. Once, while traveling, he encountered a man chasing an ox that was panting with its tongue hanging out.
Ji stopped his carriage and ordered an official to ask the man, "How many li has the ox traveled? Some criticized him, saying that such matters were irrelevant to the road.

Regarding those who died in a mass brawl, there was confusion as to whether they had perished before or after [the specific time]. Ji said, "It is currently spring, when the Yang energy of the Lesser Yang (Shao-yang) is active;
it cannot yet be intensely hot. Now that these oxen are panting, the heat must be extreme. I fear there will be injury. The Chancellor arose and regulated the Yin and Yang.
The office was in charge of summer; therefore, he questioned him. ○ Regarding "the death at the Hall of Qi," see the previous section.
○ "Either resting or moving": the *Shi Jing*, "Wu Yang" (No Sheep), says: "Some descend to the hills; some drink from the ponds; some rest, some move. The commentary states:
"Moving (*e*) means to stir. ○ "Under the Peach Forest": the *Shu Jing*, "Wu Cheng" (The Completion of Wu), says: "He released the oxen into the wilds of the Peach Forest."
It is shown that the whole world finds no relief;
pestilence and acute illnesses fail to heal, truly intensifying the anxieties of every household. Only the Buddha’s universal response can extinguish the calamities of the six portents.

I have thus exhausted my humble sincerity and offered this special, earnest prayer. I reflect deeply that I, [Name], recently possessed a body as ephemeral as a bubble or a shadow, yet was suddenly afflicted by the miasma of pestilence.
In discerning the transmission and transformation of the disease, who among us is a skilled physician like Zhang Zhongjing?

In diagnosing the floating or sinking pulses, who possesses the subtle mastery of Hua Tuo’s disciple, Wang Shuhe? Can it be said that this is merely brought about by heavenly calamity? In truth, it concerns the deficiencies inherent in human affairs.

Having already increased the transgressions recorded in the Black Register, it is only right that we incur the reprimand of the Imperial Firmament. Thus, with a heart poured forth in earnest supplication, we specifically request our lives to pray for grace.

(Enter for the Buddhist service: We humbly pray that you rescue us from this life-threatening peril as if treating a fatal ailment, and disperse the vital harmony throughout our meridians and vessels.
Grant us amnesty from ten thousand deaths, so that we need not trouble you with a "recipe for the dead"; bestow upon us the gift of rebirth, truly relying on your benevolence in cherishing life.

...of his profound virtue. ○ The six calamities (*liù lì*) are seen above. ○ Bubbles and shadows are seen in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. ○ Plague and pestilence (*zhá cāi*) are seen above.
○ Zhōngjǐng Zhāng Jī: his courtesy name was Zhōngjǐng; a native of Nányáng during the Later Han dynasty. He authored the *Shānghān Lùn* (Treatise on Cold Damage). Physician.
His knowledge was thus fully perfected; even Bian Que and Cang Gong could not surpass him. Later generations hailed him as the Sage of Medicine. Shu He Wang:

Shu He Wang was a native of Gaoping during the Western Jin dynasty. He served as the Grand Physician-in-Chief. By nature he was profound and tranquil, possessing extensive mastery of the classics and histories.
He investigated the Way of Medicine with great precision and possessed deep insight into the arts of cultivation. The Black Register. The Sovereign Vault beholds [all].
*Shang*. ○ Regarding "critical" (*weiji*), the *Wenxuan* commentary states: Xiang [Zong] said, "Critical" means precarious and urgent.

○ Regarding "the vital spots" (*gāohuáng*), the *Zuozhuan*, Year Ten of Duke Cheng, says: The Duke of Jin was ill and sought a physician from Qin. The Lord of Qin sent the physician Huan to treat him.
Before he had arrived, the Duke dreamed that his illness took the form of two upright youths (*shùzǐ*) who said: "He is a skilled physician; he fears harming me. I...
How can one escape it? One [response] says: "If you dwell above the blind and below the grease, what can be done for me?
A physician arrives and says: "The illness is incurable. From the *Chonghe* section of the *Liezi*: "That which is light and clear rises above to become Heaven;

that which is heavy and turbid sinks below to become Earth; the harmonious and vital breath (*chonghe qi*) becomes humanity. The commentary states: "Yang energy is light and clear and rises above to become..."
Heaven is the turbid and heavy Yin energy that descends to become Earth. The energies of Yin and Yang harmonize and unite to form human beings;
"Chong" (the Central Harmony) also signifies harmony. Regarding the *Jingluo* (Vascular Channels), the *Yiwenzhi* (Bibliographic Treatise) of the *Han Shu* states:

"The Medical Classics (*yijing*) originate from the human blood vessels, channels, veins, bones, and marrow, as well as Yin and Yang, the exterior and interior. They give rise to the root of the hundred ailments and the distinction between life and death. Furthermore—
The five viscera and six bowels have twelve channels and fifteen network vessels. [This concerns] praying for blessings at the Gate of Grace and praying for male progeny.

Though you dwell in quiescence, you are able to respond; I reverently pray for the auspicious signs of descending upon this mountain. If there is resonance, it must be communicated; I beseech you to grant the blessings of this prayer.

I specifically present this according to the teachings of the Elephant (Buddhism), hoping for your vast grace. I reflect deeply that I, [Name], together with my wife [Name], have long been in harmonious union like the lute and its strings, yet we have not yet dreamed of the Bear and the Tiger (the birth of a son).
My parents’ bloodline must not be abruptly severed by me; how could I bear to [interrupt] the bright sacrifices of a hundred generations?

That they are suddenly abandoned today must be due to the obstruction caused by past transgressions; thus, before the signs of birth have even manifested, I bring forth the humble mind of an ordinary person to specifically entrust myself to the Great Vow of our Buddha.
(Entering the Merit and Establishing the Vow) I humbly pray that the young phoenix may come to alight and the jade scepters may be handled;

that the ancestral lineage shall be continued without fail, so as to instantly dispel the anxieties of Bo Dao; and that there shall be radiance at the family threshold, hoping to bring about [auspicious results].
The Celebration of Mount Yan.

From the *Mao Shi*, "Song of the High Mountains" (*Sōnggāo wéiyuè*): "Lofty and high are the mountains, reaching their utmost height to the heavens. From these mountains descend spirits, giving birth to the Fūs and the Shēns.
These Shēns and Fūs are the pillars of the Zhou; they act as a bulwark for the four states and proclaim [the Way] throughout the four quarters."
○ Regarding the prayer at Mount Niqu: The *Records of the Grand Historian* (*Shiji*) states that Zhengzai prayed at Mount Niqu and gave birth to Confucius.
○ Regarding the "Elephant Teaching" (*Xiangjiao*): See above. ○ Regarding the "Bear and Wolf" (*Xiongpi*) from the "Sigan" (*Sikan*) poem:
"Sleeping and rising, I divined my dream. What was the auspicious dream? It was of a bear and a wolf; it was of a viper and a snake. The great man divined it: it was..."

The bear and the brown bear are omens of a male child; the viper and the serpent are omens of a female child. *Note on the "Mingyin" (Pure Sacrifice) in the "Luo Gao":* Mingyin refers to a pure and solemn sacrifice.
Regarding the *juezhu* (pheasant-king): the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is a divine bird belonging to the species of the *feng* (phoenix).
Regarding the *gui* (jade scepter) and *zhang* (circular jade): the *Shi Jing*, "Sigan" (*Sigan* ode), says: "When a male child is born, he is laid upon the bed. He is...
He wears the lower garment; he carries the jade scepter. His weeping resounds loudly. *Bo Dao* refers to Deng You of the Jin dynasty, whose courtesy name was Bo Dao.
He served as the Governor of Hedong. When he fell into the hands of Shi Le, he cut his carriage to pieces and fled with his wife and children, carrying them on oxen and horses.
He was subsequently encountered by bandits who plundered his oxen and horses; he then fled on foot, carrying his son and his younger brother.
The son, unable to fulfill both duties, said to his wife, "My younger brother died young, leaving only this one child;
it is not right for his lineage to be cut off. I must abandon my own son so that he may survive. If he is spared, I shall surely have children later.
His wife wept but followed his wish, and he abandoned his own son. Later, he indeed ended up without heirs. At that time, people praised him for his righteousness.
Lamenting this, he said: "The Way of Heaven is without consciousness; it has caused Deng Baidao to have no son. [This concludes] "Yanshan Sees the Emperor Above.
[This concludes] "The Lute and Zither Have Long Been in Harmony" Part Two, with the note on obtaining a male child after childbirth.
Having obtained this succession, I return to fulfill my vow;

though the omens of the bear and the *pí* had not yet appeared, I previously established an oath to pray for grace. Now that the bow and arrows are suspended, I perform the rites to repay your virtue.
With utmost reverence and sincerity, I am truly joyful and delighted. I humbly reflect that [Name], my fellow resident, has committed offenses as heavy as mountains, yet through your virtue...
Light as wings, I have not yet seen the joy of a single son; I am deeply burdened by the anxiety of the three unfilialities.
Only our Buddha, bestowing compassion, can fulfill these two prayers; thus, when the commoner below prays, he is granted the grace of a single child.

To honor my former vow, I specifically repay this myriad protection. (Enter for the ritual) I humbly pray that the orchids and cassias shall bloom together in fragrance, and that the blessings of the *zhongsī* shall flourish and spread.
Once born and nurtured, the perspiration from the jade branches shall be forever gathered; may they be long-lived and flourish, so that the anxieties of the golden chains shall not obstruct them.
Regarding the bear and the *pí* (a type of large bear), and the bow and arrow, both are seen above. "First drawing for a son": The *Yi Zhuan*, "Explanation of the Hexagrams," says:
"Zhen draws once and obtains a son; therefore it is called the eldest son. Xun draws once and obtains a daughter; therefore it is called the eldest daughter."
On Filial Piety. III. Regarding the three forms of unfiliality, Mencius said: "There are three forms of unfiliality; failing to continue one's lineage is the greatest. Commentary by Master Zhao:
According to the rites, there are three matters that constitute unfiliality: first, to flatter one's parents and follow their whims, thereby leading them into unrighteousness;
second, to remain unemployed when the family is poor and the parents are old; and third, not to marry or have children, thereby severing the ancestral line.

The third is sacrifice (*śrāddha*). Among these three, the absence of the latter is considered the greatest [transgression]. Second, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) states: First is the "seeking of acquisition" (*lābha-paryeṣaṇā*).

This refers to all sentient beings desiring to obtain various pleasures and seeking them according to their wishes; even when passing through dangers and hardships, they do not consider them suffering.
Like the ocean swallowing rivers, their minds never reach satiety—this is called the seeking of acquisition. Second is the "seeking of life" (*jīvita-paryeṣaṇā*).

This refers to sentient beings who, grasping at pleasure, give rise to craving; they are unable to observe with reality as it is that pleasure is the cause of suffering, yet instead seek long life to experience these various pleasures.
This is called "seeking life. The *Mao Shi* (Poetry of Mao) says of the *zhōngsī* (locust):
"The wings of the *zhōngsī* flutter in swarms; may your descendants be numerous and vigorous. The commentary states: "The *zhōngsī* belongs to the class of locusts; one birth..."
Ninety-nine Sons. ○ *Yuzhi* (Jade Branch). From the *Han Wudi Ji*: The Emperor obtained a jade branch from the kingdom of Sina and bestowed it upon his senior ministers, saying:
"If one falls ill, the branch will sweat; if one dies, the branch will break.
Lao Dan possessed it for seven hundred years without it sweating; Woquan possessed it for three thousand years without it breaking. ○ *Jinsuo* (Golden Lock).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is like being confined in a prison and shackled with fetters; even if one receives a pardon, to be bound again by golden chains.
Human beings are bound by craving as if in a prison; though they have left the household life, to further adhere to restrictive precepts is like being bound by golden chains."

The preservation of the fetus and the birth of offspring are matters of vital concern to the family. That prayers may be answered so as to avert calamities arising from the unprovoked is a sincere hope.
I therefore respectfully submit this written petition to express my feelings, and reverently perform the Buddhist rites to invoke blessings. I, [Name], reflect that my pregnant wife, [Name] Fan...

Of humble substance like duckweed and of fragile frame like the *púliù* tree, as I approach the time to lie upon my sickbed, I am deeply moved by the thought of [the Buddha’s] compassion reaching even to the mulberry trees.
That the bear and the wolf appeared in a dream leaves me still in a state of hesitation; that the serpent and the viper presented an auspicious sign likewise places me within the realm of doubt.
I pray only for the two characters "security and peace," and how could I dare forget to pay reverence to the Triple Gem? (Insert Buddhist ritual or take a vow) I humbly pray that my wife (Name)...
The birth is auspicious and there is no peril upon the matting; the auspicious response is a son as precious as a pearl in the palm, bringing joy that fills the family home.
As the fragrant blossoms open like the courtyard osmanthus, how soon shall we see the peace of his arrival at the maternal residence?
○ *Jiaren* (Family): The hexagram *Jiaren*. "In the family, it is advantageous for the woman to be correct. Commentary: "The way of the family finds its advantage in the correctness of the woman.
When the woman is correct, the way of the family becomes correct. ○ *Wuwang* (Sincerity Without Deception), top line. ○ *Puliu* (Poplar and Willow) from the *Shuowen*:
Gu Kaizhi was the same age as Emperor Jianwen, yet his hair turned white early. When asked the reason for this, he replied: [text missing]
The character of the pine and cypress becomes more lush after enduring winter; the nature of the *pú* and *liù* trees withers prematurely at the sight of autumn.
○ *Chè sāng* (Cutting the mulberry) ○ *Xióng pí* (Bears and tigers) are both seen above. ○ Regarding *yóu-èr*: the *Erya* says that *yóu* is the name of a beast. Its form resembles a [chén-máng].
It is skilled at climbing trees and is by nature full of suspicion and hesitation. It usually dwells in the mountains; if it suddenly hears a sound, it immediately becomes fearful.
It came to harm him. Every time [the man] anticipated this, he would climb up a tree; after a long while and seeing no one else, only then did he dare to descend.
In a short moment he would climb up again. This happened more than once; thus, that which is not yet decided is called "hesitation" (*yù*). ○ Regarding snakes and vipers, see the previous entry.
○ Regarding "fox-doubt" (*huxi*), the *Han shu*, Annals of Emperor Wen, notes: "The fox is a beast whose nature is full of suspicion.
Whenever it crosses an icy river, it listens as it steps. Therefore, one who is hesitant is called 'fox-doubting'.
○ Regarding "palm-jewel" (*zhāngzhū*), Du Ji’s poem to the Prince of Hanzhong says: "In my palm, I discover a newly found pearl. (Note: This refers to the person Ma Fanhe.)
Yu You said, "It is as if one has obtained a jade from within the palm of one's hand. ○ Regarding Chong-lu:
when Jia Chong was first born, his father remarked that there would later be a celebration of prosperity filling the gates of the household; thus he was named accordingly.

The commentary notes that those who have attained eminent rank and nobility throughout history have had their gates and courtyards filled with guests. This means that in the future, this child shall likewise be so. Later, it indeed came to pass.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Western Jin, he served as Minister of Works (*Sikong*) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lu. Regarding the protocols for entering the residence, the *Neize* states:
"When a wife is about to give birth, or when her month of confinement has arrived, she goes to the side chamber."
Having given birth to a son, I fulfill my vow;

may the bear and the grizzly bear appear in my dreams, so that I may hope to avert the calamity of the "thorny chamber. With these ants and leeches repaying their grace, I pray to reach the ears of the Awakened Sovereign.
I reflect deeply that my wife, [Name], is of extremely frail constitution and her destiny has been fraught with many misfortunes. Recently, as the month of childbirth arrived...

Xiang: Truly, one must exercise greater caution than when treading on thin ice. Zhang: One hopes that the child may be played with for years, so that the heart may find peace while resting upon the pillow.
Zhu: One desires to hold it up again, yet it has not yet entered the palms to be gazed upon. This is truly the great fortune of a Sage; we hope it will preserve the safety of the Little Lord.

Having received this new grace, how could I dare forget my former vow? (Entering for the rite of returning vows) I humbly pray that the lute and zither may harmonize in their resonance, and that the fragrance of the cassia and orchid may spread afar.
May we behold the joy of one who brings honor to the family—long life and health—and may the capability of the one who manages the household lead to prosperity and flourishing growth.
○ "Bears and cubs" refers to what appears above. ○ "Jing-shi" (荊室) refers to calling one's own wife "Jing-shi. ○ "Ants and leeches" refers to what appears above.

within [the house], there is no child even five feet tall who is capable of attending to the household gate.)

Having given birth to a daughter and fulfilled her vow, she recalls the former dream of the *táng* flower during her pregnancy and thus knocks at the gate of the Awakened Sovereign (*Buddha*). Now, to express her sincerity with offerings of wild herbs, she reverently practices the Buddhist scriptures.
She reflects deeply that her wife, [Name], as the time of her great delivery approached, was consumed solely by the anxiety for herself alone. Although she was humble...

The birth of daughters and the conception of sons each proceed from the creative forces of Heaven and Earth; yet Qian is designated as Father and Kun as Mother, so that the process of generation may be fulfilled.

Thus, having purified oneself through ritual bathing, one establishes a solemn covenant, and indeed the auspiciousness of childbirth ensues. Therefore, we present this Buddhist teaching to express our particular gratitude for this profound bounty.

(I enter the matter of returning vows: I prostrate myself and pray that your auspicious blessings may be ever more exalted and your gracious favors eternally abundant. Having been born and nurtured, we have already attained the joy of domestic harmony;
now that they have grown and matured, I pray that the excellence of our household may soon be fulfilled.
The dream of the *táng* flower is seen in the Appendix below. The sincerity of the *qín* herb is [discussed] above. That *Xùn* obtains the female and *Zhèn* obtains the male is also seen above.

Regarding the excellence of the inner quarters, Zhang Xuan of the Jin dynasty had a younger sister of talent and substance who married the Gu family; Zhang Xuan frequently praised her as being the equal of Wang Ningzhi’s wife, Xie Daoyun. [Zhi] Ji.
Nie said: "The Countess Wang’s spirit and demeanor were relaxed and expansive; thus she possessed the air of one who dwells beneath the forest.
The lady of the Gu family was fresh and pure, like the radiance of jade; she was truly a beauty of the inner chambers. (Note: The Countess Wang is Dao Yun.

Prayer for the Peace of an Infant (Applicable to those using adopted surnames or making vows, etc.):

Affection is concentrated upon this child; first, I am concerned for his state of ignorance. I pray with sincerity to the Buddha, the Awakened Sovereign, that he may preemptively dispel this groundless illness.
I respectfully present these few lines of paper to express my humble thoughts. I reflect deeply that I, [Name], together with my wife, [Name], are not superior to others in virtue;
yet we have always anticipated matters with forethought. Fortunately, we have been blessed with the joy of a son; privately, I hoped he would possess the capability to excel his father.

However, as he has not been at peace since infancy, I fear deeply that there may be the calamity of the Five Elements mutually overcoming one another. As there have been many obstructions during his nursing, I am acutely concerned that the Three Life-destinies (*sanming*) may suffer from physical conflict.

...this calamity. Thus, moved by the ancient counsel of "preparing for the mulberry before the leaves fall," I have specially offered my sincere devotion toward the Sun [of Wisdom]. Therefore, (entering into the Buddhist rite), I prostrate myself with the vow:
may You take pity on this frail body and protect this humble life. May my destiny never encounter stagnation, but always meet Amitāyus Buddha;

may the foundation of my merit be forever firm, and may I constantly encounter King Prabhūtaratna. May this truly become a source of auspiciousness for sustaining the family legacy, and may it greatly increase the prosperity within my gates.

I pray that upon entering school, you will establish your vows and reflect:

I, [Name], am a lowly subject from the grass and weeds, a humble scholar who merely occupies himself with the brush and tablets. Though I have labored diligently over the yellow scrolls, I have not yet attained the understanding of human relations.
I, [Name], whose aspirations soar toward the azure clouds, have long contemplated the means to set my career in motion.

Now that I am about to undergo examination and the date for the test approaches, I have reverently prepared these ritual offerings and respectfully approach the presence of [Title] at [Location] to request your favor regarding [my vow].

I pray that my literary brilliance may rival the radiance of five-layered clouds and that my thoughts may surge like waves from ten thousand streams. May auspicious signs illuminate the school hall, and may my merit be happily inscribed in the registers of Confucius.
His reputation was already established early on at the schools of Zhou, like light floating over the waters of the Pan River.

Regarding the phrase "occupying the *bi* and studying the records," it says: "Those who teach today merely chant over what they occupy and view in their *bi*, multiplying their interrogations. The commentary notes: "*Zhan*" means to look;
"*bi*" refers to bamboo slips (the ancient tablets). This means that those who teach people today do nothing but recite and intone the bamboo slips upon which they gaze.
