○ *Qingyunzhi* refers to the "Preface to the Pavilion of the Prince of Xi. ○ Regarding the term *faren* (setting out): the pronunciation of *ren* is *rin*.

The *ren* is the wooden block that obstructs the wheels. Once the *ren* is removed, the wheels turn and the carriage moves; therefore, when anything is first undertaken, it is called "setting out from the *ren*" (*fā rèn*).
This is seen in the *Chuci*. *Hénggōng* (黌宮): The character for *héng* is pronounced *huáng*; it refers to a school building. *Lùjí* (魯籍):

The character for *jí* is pronounced *jì*; it refers to official registers or ledgers. Regarding the *Pànshuǐ* (泮水) of the *Shijing*: "Joyfully we delight in the Pàn. [The text continues: "The Pàn water... [etc.]

"Water. The commentary states: "The waters of the *pàn* (shallow pool). These are the waters of the *pàngōng* (the Hall of the Half-Moon). The schools of the feudal lords, the halls for the ritual archery of the districts, are called *pàngōng*.
To the east, south, and west, there are bodies of water shaped like half-moons. Because they are half the size of the [circular] *bìyōng* (encircling pond)."

I humbly submit this vow of gratitude upon entering the academy. That honor has now fallen upon my humble thatched door, serving as the initial departure for a soaring career like that of the great Peng bird;

may its radiance shine upon the waters of the Confucian college, acting as a herald for future success in the Han Garden (the literary court). Thus, I exhaust my ant-like sincerity to repay your vast protection. I, [Name], reflect deeply that my studies have been focused exclusively on the mastery of the bamboo slips.

Having practiced the craft of "carving insects" (poetry), I have applied my mind with diligence at the "chicken-window" (the study) in the hope of being selected for the "green coins" (the imperial examination).

Having turned my heart toward the lion-throne (the Buddha), I was subsequently enrolled in the ranks of the school. Fearing that I might long fail my former vow, I hereby humbly present this expression of my innermost sincerity. (Entering for the rite of returning a vow.
I pray that you may achieve renown in the garden of arts and make your mark in the literary arena, so that you may fortunately serve as a guest in the house of the host and behold the Great View.
Shining upon the imperial court, he rejoices in being enrolled in the registers of office, spreading his wings upon the celestial highway.

He traveled about with his books tucked under his arm. (The note states: "tucking the divining stalks" refers to holding a scroll.

Regarding "carving insects": The *Fáyán* of Yang Xiong says: Someone asked, "Do you, sir, enjoy the *fù* style? He replied, "Indeed. As a child, I carved insects and engraved seals. After a while, he added, "A man of mature strength does not do such things.

Chu Zong purchased a long-crowing rooster and cherished it with extreme care, always keeping it by the window.

Later, the rooster spoke in human language and engaged in conversation with Chu Zong, discussing matters at great length without ceasing all day long. Because of this, Chu Zong’s achievements and career advanced significantly.
*Qingqian Zhang Zu*, courtesy name Wencheng, was a person of the reign of Emperor Gaozong who participated in the *zhiju* (preparation-based examinations).

He passed all the examinations. The official Ban Qian remarked that his writings were like bronze coins: "Ten thousand selections, ten thousand hits. Thus, he was called the "Green Coin Scholar" (Qingqian Xueshi).
Regarding the hexagram Guan (Contemplation), the fourth line of the lower trigram states: "One contemplates the light of the state; it is advantageous to serve as a guest at the court of the King.

His traces follow the rarefied path of Chao Fu and Xu You; he soars beyond the mundane realm to spread his wings, transcending the celestial highway to stand loftily aloft.

As the autumn examination is established and the autumn wind first blows, it coincides precisely with the season for riding the wind. As the autumn cassia is about to bloom, he joyfully cherishes the aspiration of plucking its branches.

I pray that the examination hall may be blessed with auspiciousness, and I hope that Your Holiness’s sacred power will bestow further grace. Reflecting deeply, I, [Name], devoted myself to the *Lunyu* in my youth and have since been a mere pretender at the Zhou Academy.

Stuck in the dim light of the "chicken-window" (my study), I have repeatedly failed to realize my ambition to ascend the clouds; laboring over these decayed scrolls, I have often felt the urge to snatch the prize of the brocade.
Now that the time has arrived for me to spread my wings and the day draws near for me to spur on my steed, I do not dare fail to beseech the protection of your myriad-roofed pavilion.

May you safely secure the merit of these three battles. (Upon entering, he makes this vow: I humbly pray that your brush may paint with the brilliance of the five clouds, and your thoughts flow like waves of ten thousand bushels.

May the ink on the Tiger Roll be fresh as you joyfully become the leader among those from Southern Min; may the fragrance of the Moon Palace blossom as you swiftly receive the imperial grace of the Northern Gate.
Furthermore, I pray for success and profit upon your departure, freedom from peril at every stage, and auspiciousness throughout your journey there and back. May your person be ever well.
The mind is at ease.

Regarding the "Qionglin" (Jade Forest): the court banquet bestowed upon those who have passed the jinshi examination is called the Qionglin Banquet.
In the eighth year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song dynasty, Song Bai and others were all granted the degree and bestowed with a banquet;
it was first held at the Qionglin Garden, and subsequently became an established custom. Regarding the "Golden Plaque": the *Xijing Zaji* states that Cui Shao died suddenly but returned to life.
I saw a list of names inscribed in the underworld: those destined for the rank of Chancellor or General were on a golden plaque; those of the next rank were on a silver plaque;

and officials of the prefectures and counties were all on iron plaques. Regarding "Shanglin" (Upper Forest): in the commentary to the *Shanglin Fu* (Rhapsody on the Upper Forest), Liang says it is the name of the Shanglin Garden.
Regarding the "Feast at Qujiang": Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty constructed Qujiang Pond. Its waters bend to the west. During the Tang dynasty...

On the Shangsi festival, people would go to the head of Qujiang to drink by the stream and enjoy the spring outing. Emperor Minghuang posthumously enfeoffed Zhang Jiuling here, bestowing upon him the title "Lord of Qujiang.
Later, when scholars of outstanding talent passed the examinations, they were granted a banquet here.

In spring, I established my vows to enter the Imperial Academy, aspiring to achieve victory within the thorny enclosure; in autumn, I offered my sincere devotion at the ritual sacrifice, seeking the grace of the Lotus Throne.

Thus I have established this noble covenant, hoping for your compassionate discernment. I humbly reflect that I, [Name], am but a lowly student of the brush, a common material of no use like the *chū* and *lì* trees.

Though my diligent efforts were like the glow of a firefly, they failed to reach the path of the azure clouds; yet, through the recommendation of a famous eagle, I have fortunately partaken in the fragrance of the vermilion cassia.

Still, I hope to illuminate the peach waves to soar upward; how could I bear to let the splendor of the apricot blossoms go to waste? Therefore, I rely upon the monastic community to take refuge in the Imperial Awakening.
I humbly pray that Yang’s prose may emit phoenixes and Li’s brush may give birth to flowers, so that I may be the first to ascend the golden scroll. What need is there for further words?

A scholar who has long been hidden within his bag has now won the first prize at the silken banner, truly deserving the title of an elite who has entered the target. We further pray that you may enjoy prosperity on both your outward and return journeys, and that your body and mind remain ever at ease.
May you have no cause for anxiety upon setting out, and encounter no misfortune upon reaching your destination.
The *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), in the section on the Minister of Spring (*Chunguan Zongbo*), states: "The Minister of Spring presides over the rites. The commentary notes:

"The Minister of Spring is a high minister (*qing*) who presides over the state rites. He manages affairs concerning the celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, and ancestral ghosts, harmonizing the relations between superiors and subordinates, and between the honorable and the humble.
As the Minister of Spring is ranked as the foremost among the sequence of the four seasons, his office is called 'Zongbo' (Ancestral Patriarch). — *Jikui Tongdian*.

It is said: On the day of the examination for the selection of candidates by the Ministry of Rites, military guards were strictly stationed and thorny branches were used to encircle the area to prevent the inclusion of those who were fraudulent or spurious.
(Note: "Jian" means to encircle; "jia-lan" refers to those who falsely assume the guise [of talent] or those who enter in an indiscriminate manner.

On the day of the examination, military guards were deployed with strict vigilance and the site was surrounded with thorns to prevent the admission of those who feign talent or those who have entered improperly. *Zhanbi* (Occupying the Writing Brush): [This term refers to the act of studying or writing.]
○ *Chū* and *Ryaku* are both mentioned above. ○ Regarding the light of the firefly: Jin Che Yin (style name:
Wuzi), a native of Nanping, was diligent and tireless in his studies, possessing broad and comprehensive knowledge. Being poor, he could not always afford oil;
during the summer months, he would fill a silk pouch with dozens of fireflies to use as a lamp while reading. Thus, he continued his studies from night until day. ○ The path to the blue clouds.
Song Liang Hao passed the imperial examination as the *zhuangyuan* (first-place graduate). At the age of eighty-two, he presented this letter of thanks:
"With white hair, I have exhausted my studies of the classics; I am eight years younger than Fu Sheng. Having found my path to the blue clouds, I am two years older than Lü Shang.

After Mi Heng was recommended by the "eagle" (a metaphor for a patron), he was only in his early twenties. Kong Rong, admiring his talent, submitted a memorial to recommend him, saying: "A bird of prey... [accumulates... [its strength].
"A hundred are not equal to one osprey. Had [Zhang] Heng been established at court, there would surely have been something admirable to behold.
○ *Dan-gui* (The Red Cassia) and *Tao-lang* (The Peach Waves) are both seen above. ○ *Xinghua* (Peach Blossom): Zhuangzi says, "Confucius was traveling through the forests of Zhi and Wei;
he rested upon the Terrace of Peach Blossoms (*Xingtán*), where he read books, sang songs, and played the zither. ○ Yang Wen's "Spitting Phoenixes" (*Hòuhàn*).
Yang Xiong, courtesy name Ziyun, lived during the reign of Emperor Cheng. At that time, there was a guest who recommended Yang Xiong’s writings, noting they resembled those of Sima Xiangru.
The Emperor summoned Xiong to serve as a court attendant at the Chéngmíng courtyard. Upon his return, he presented the *Gānquán Fù* (Rhapsody on Gānquán) as a memorial to offer encouragement.

When Xiong finished composing the *Gānquán Fù*, he dreamed of vomiting forth a white phoenix. Regarding Li Bai, the *Tiānbǎo Yíshì* (Anecdotes from the Tiānbǎo Era) states: "Li Bai’s pen grew flowers."

In his youth, he dreamed that flowers grew from the tip of his writing brush; from then on, his literary talent and thought progressed daily. He was subsequently seen atop the Golden List (the imperial examination rankings).
Regarding the "scholar within the bag," the *Biography of Lord Pingyuan of Shiji* states: Lord Pingyuan of the State of Zhao sought to form a military alliance at Chu.
There were nineteen guests present. Mao Sui volunteered himself, saying: "When I am placed within a sack like a锥 (a conical awl), it thrusts its point out;
it is not merely that I have not yet been seen. [The phrase] "winning the first prize in the brocade banner" appears above.
"Outstanding Talents Who Have Entered the Bowstring": During the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, he visited the Duan Gate in private.
Seeing the jinshi candidates emerging in a procession, he said with delight, "The heroes of the world have all entered my bowstring. (Note:
*Gu* means to draw a bow to its full extent; "entering the bowstring" is a metaphor for falling into one's trap.)

Having ascended the ladder of success, I return to fulfill my vow; the spring is thick within the Apricot Garden, rejoicing in the warm waves of the Dragon Gate. With the swift report of victory from the thorny enclosure, I receive the fresh grace of the Phoenix Palace.

Formerly I relied upon your vast bounty; now I diligently offer this ant-like repayment. I humbly reflect that my resolve was bitter beneath the green lamp, and my labor diligent over the yellow scrolls.
Toiling through heat and cold, how could one harbor cravings for mere warmth and fullness? Diligently through day and night, one contemplates exerting oneself toward fame and achievement.

Fortunate to have partaken in the radiance of the *yanta* (the Imperial Academy), all of this belongs to the protection of the *siṃhāsana* (the Lion Throne). Thus, reflecting upon how to repay this kindness, how could I not be refined and devout?
I, [Name], humbly pray that the imperial grace may ever increase and that my duties as a subject remain ever vigilant.
May my green robe and jade tablet forever encircle the dignity of the North Star, and may my purple sash and golden fish forever offer blessings for the longevity of the Southern Mountain.
Regarding "Longmen" (Dragon Gate): Longmen is a metaphor for fish. It refers to the mouth where the waters of the Longmen River descend;
it is located in present-day Longmen County, Jiangzhou. The waters of Longmen are so treacherous and impassable that fish and turtles of all kinds cannot ascend them.
Thousands of large fish from the rivers and seas gather beneath the Dragon Gate, but none can pass over. Once they have ascended, they become dragons.

Nowadays, when a scholar is received with such courtesy and hospitality, it is said that he has "ascended the Dragon Gate. This account is found in the biography of Li Ying during the Eastern Han dynasty.
*Jiwei* (surrounded by thorns), *Yibao* (the ant's repayment), and *Huangjuan* (yellow scrolls) are all seen above.
*Keke*: In the *Wenxuan*, Li Zhouhan’s commentary states it means "diligent labor. Furthermore, in the *Guifan* commentary, it is glossed as "laboring to the extreme. *Wen* (warmth).
"Having seen Mencius fully. "Zealous for Mencius" (note): the meaning is one of diligent application. "The Goose Pagoda" (*Xiyu ji*):
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who saw a pair of geese flying. Suddenly, one goose dropped down and perished.
The assembly said, "This goose has offered us a warning; we should commemorate its virtue. Thereupon, they erected a pagoda [shaped like] a goose. Furthermore, in ancient times...
Now, the *Shihua* (Discourse on Poetry) says: When Wei Zhao of the Tang dynasty attained the jinshi degree, he happened to inscribe his name upon the Crane Pagoda at Ci’en Monastery.
Later generations emulated him, and it thus became an established custom. The *Zishou Qian Baiguan Biao* (Purple Ribbons: A Table of the Former Hundred Officials) states:

"The Chancellor wears a gold seal and purple ribbons. The commentary notes: "Ribbons (*shou*) are the cords for wearing seals. Regarding the "Golden Fish," the *Tang Shu* (History of the Tang) states: [Emperor] Gaozong...
Silver fish pouches were granted to those of the fifth rank and above for personal use, to prevent fraud regarding summons; they had to be matched when entering or leaving the palace.
Those of the third rank and above were provided with gold-ornamented pouches. During the Chuánggǒng era, the *dūdu* and *cìshǐ* (prefectural governors) first began to be granted the fish insignia.
In the second year of the Tiānshòu era, the fish-shaped pendants were all changed to tortoises. Subsequently, the tortoise bags of those of the third rank and above were adorned with gold;
those of the fourth rank with silver; and those of the fifth rank with copper. At the beginning of Zhōngzōng’s reign, the tortoise bags were abolished, and the fish pendants were restored.
Regarding the longevity of the Southern Mountains, the *Tiānbão* (Heavenly Protection) ode says: "May your longevity be like the Southern Mountains—unwavering and unimpaired."

The Emperor has passed away. As officials depart for their posts, we pray for the security of the imperial grace, which is now all the more weighty; how could we dare disdain the toil of the journey? My own office is especially difficult, and I truly harbor anxieties as grave as ice and abyss.
I burn this incense to pay my respects and present these few sheets of paper to pray for peace and security.

I, [Name], reflect that having been granted entry into the registers of officials and having presumptuously joined the ranks of ministers, I have received this mandate as a matter of honor and ought not to delay in preparing my journey.

Yet, I fear that the vessels and carriages may not be favorable and that bandits are currently rampant; furthermore, I am concerned that local customs differ and treacherous enemies are unpredictable. Therefore, I earnestly entreat Your Sacred Compassion.

Under its protection, may the anxieties of this humble official post be eased. (Entering for the Buddhist service: We humbly pray that you remain unharmed on your travels and that all be peaceful in your office.

May you perpetually sustain the flourishing light of your virtue so as not to disgrace your station; may we soon behold the decree of your honorable promotion and receive extensively the extraordinary blessings thereof.

Regarding the toil of traveling over land and water, the *Shi* (Book of Odes), in the "Dai Chi" (Far and Wide), says: "The high official travels on foot and wades through water; my heart is filled with anxiety. The commentary notes:
"Traveling on grassy ground is called 'ba' (treading); traveling through water is called 'she' (wading). Regarding anxieties concerning ice and deep pools, see the previous section.

Regarding the ritual of bowing upon receiving a command, the *Zuo Zhuan*, year eleven of Duke Zhuang, says: "I bow for the honor of receiving your command. The commentary notes: "This is to express gratitude for the honor of your generous decree. Regarding preparing one's luggage (*chuzhuang*), [the text continues].

In Zhang Pingzi’s *Sīxuán fǔ* (Rhapsody on Contemplating the Mysterious), it says: "I selected an auspicious day to set out on my journey. Li Shàn’s commentary states: "Chù means 'to begin. Regarding "wúyàng" (no ailment):
The *Shényì jīng* (Scripture of Divine Marvels) says, "In the north there is a beast called [狂-王+恙]. It is the same as 'yàng' (ailment). The Yellow Emperor killed it;
from then on, people had no grief or illness, and thus it was called 'wúyàng' (no ailment)."

Having prayed for peace and safety upon taking up his official post and subsequently fulfilled his vow, the official reflected that the path of service is fraught with perils; thus, he conceived the thought of crossing over these difficulties. Relying on the boundless power of the Sage, he fortunately obtained the auspiciousness of constancy.

Desiring to repay the compassionate protection [bestowed upon me], I have exhausted my humble sincerity. I reflect deeply that I am ashamed to behold the imperial splendor and lack the ability to serve while drawing a salary.
On this ten-thousand-li journey, I already feel the urgency of the fear of failing in my duties; yet at this moment of receiving the manifest decree, I harbor profound anxiety and trepidation.
Thus, the words of the covenant were established, and the fruit indeed responded like an echo. Recalling the sincerity of years past, we now exhaust our reverence of this day.
(Entering for the Buddhist service) We humbly pray that you grant us a great year and bestow upon us vast blessings. May they come as rivers flow in;
may we repeatedly receive the honor of the Imperial Edict like the rising sun, and joyfully behold the Emperor’s countenance with delight.

Regarding the thought of "advantageously crossing over," the *Yi* says: "Xu: There is sincerity; brilliant success. Persistence brings good fortune. It is advantageous to cross the great river. The *Benyi* (Original Meaning) says:
"Xu means 'to wait. This is formed by Qian meeting Kan. Qian represents strength and Kan represents peril.
To encounter peril with strength yet not advance precipitously so as to fall into danger—this is the meaning of waiting. 'Sincerity' (*fu*) refers to that which is within [the heart]. [Observation]
"Light seen above. (From the *Shijing*). "Awkward and hesitant speech. (Commentary): An expression for being respectful and uneasy. "The echo responds; seeing the 'Discourse on the Fall of Qin'.
(From the *Han Feizi*). "Grant you great blessings. "Like a river just beginning to flow. Both are found in the *Mao Shi*.
"The glory of the imperial decree of the Phoenix. The *Yecheng Ji* states: "Shi Jilong was with the Empress in the Pavilion."
Above, an imperial edict was carried in the mouth of a wooden phoenix; it descended in flight, winding down hundreds of feet of crimson rope.
Like the rising sun, he was seen in the poem "Tianbao. Regarding the joy of his dragon-like countenance:
the Former Han Gaozu, whose taboo name was Bang and courtesy name Ji, was a native of Zhongyang Village in Fengyi. His surname was Liu. His mother, Lady Wang, once rested...
At the embankment of the Great Marsh, she dreamed of meeting a deity. At that time, thunder and lightning filled the air with darkness.

When her father, Grandfather Tai Gong, went there, he saw two interlacing dragons above. Shortly thereafter, she became pregnant and subsequently gave birth to the High Ancestor, who had a prominent nose and the countenance of a dragon.

Merchants travel abroad seeking safety amidst rain and wind, striving for the profit of a mere needle or blade; they gaze upon the clouds and follow the sun, hoping their drums will sound in unison with the wild boars.

We have carefully selected an auspicious day of grain to set forth our humble sincerity. I, [Name], reflect that I am ashamed to act as a hare guarding its burrow, and weary of the ceaseless flitting of a fly.
Thus he set out on his journey, deliberating and weighing his course. He reflected upon the hardships of the inn, fearing the shock of being insulted;

he also considered the perils of the traveler’s boat, apprehensive of the suffering of drowning. He endured both cold and heat for his person, while his goods were sometimes stalled and sometimes moving freely.
If one does not receive blessings from past hardships, how could one achieve success in future undertakings? (Entering the Buddhist service:
We humbly pray that You will observe our reverent devotion and bestow Your imperial discernment. May the journey by carriage and the voyage by boat alike be graced with auspicious omens;
may we set forth with empty bags and return with full bundles, thereby securing even the slightest profit.
○ Regarding "the profit of awls and knives," the *Zuo Zhuan* (Annals of Zuo), "Zhao" period, states: "They will struggle over even the tips of awls and knives.
The commentary notes that the "tips of awls and knives" are extremely fine, used as a metaphor for trivial matters. ○ "Drumsticks and drums" and "a rabbit guarding [its hole]" both appear above.

○ Regarding "the fly buzzing about," the *Mao Shi* (Poetry of Mao) says: "Buzzing, buzzing, the green fly. The commentary notes that "buzzing" describes its coming and going. ○ "Intrusion and insult."
The *Qu lǐ* says: "In ritual, one does not exceed the proper measure, nor does one encroach upon or insult others.

Regarding the line from the *Shī* (Odes), *Xiǎo mǐn*: "Like that flowing spring, do not sink together in ruin. The commentary states: "Lún" means to sink into; "xū" means mutual. "Wèiyì huánghuáng" appears above [in the previous section].
Regarding "fǎn zhōu zhī yì" (the service of ferrying boats): this refers to the thirteenth year of Duke Xī of the *Zuǒ Zhuan*, when the state of Qín [acted thus].
They transported grain to Jin, proceeding from Yong to Jiang in succession; this was designated as the "Campaign of the Floating Boats. (Note:
This refers to transporting [grain] by waterway from the Wei River into the Yellow and Fen Rivers. "Carrying empty bags and returning with full loads. The *Guoyu* states:
"The envoys of the feudal lords entered with empty bags and returned with their loads fully packed. (Note: *Kun* means a bundle.)

That merchants return their vows for profit is the harmony of righteousness; thus they attain the gains sought by the swarming fly. That sincerity is the Way of Heaven—how could I dare forget the sincerity of the ant’s repayment?
I reverently perform the Buddhist rites, strictly adhering to the teachings of the Dharma. I reflect deeply that I, [Name], have sought a livelihood in the four quarters and placed myself...

A journey of a thousand *li* has begun; the ruts of the carriage wheels stretch out like surging waters toward the ford where one’s feet find rest. The floating boat is crossing over, drifting back and forth toward the shore from which it turned its head.

Alarmed by the varying depths of human sentiment and weary of the fluctuations between the heat and cold of the world’s ways, I dare not linger, for I do not yet know when the rescue will be complete.
Desiring to gather the blessings of those on this journey, I rely solely upon the grace of Your Holiness’s protection. Now, as I turn my banner back...

At this time, I humbly express my sincere gratitude for [the gift of] the ring. (Entering the Buddhist ritual) I pray that your plans to enrich the household may be fulfilled and your schemes to support the family may succeed.

Whether walking as merchants or sitting as traders, may you all be free from the anxiety of stagnant goods; may those who produce have swift application and those who consume have leisure, so that there is always the way to generate wealth.
"Flies busying themselves over meat" (yíng yíng) and "ants returning with news" (yǐ bào) both appear above.

Regarding "making a living on the four quarters" (hú kǒu sì fāng), in the eleventh year of the Zuǒ Zhuan, the Duke of Zhèng said: "I have a younger brother named Shūduàn whom I could not harmonize with;

he has been forced to seek his livelihood on the four quarters. The commentary states that this means he caused Shūduàn to subsist by depending on the various states of the four quarters. This refers to the first year of [Shū]duàn's reign.

**Bēnggòng (奔共).** ○ *Jiānguān* (間關): The "Discourse on the Biography of Xún Yù" in the *Hòuhànshū* states: "Master Xún then crossed the Hé and Jì regions, traveling *jiānguān* to follow the Cáo clan.
The commentary notes: "*Jiānguān*" means to turn about or travel circuitously. ○ *Fǎnpài* (返斾): The *Zuǒzhuan* states:
"The Grand Minister turned his southward wheels and returned his banners (*fǎnpài*). The commentary notes: "He was about to return. ○ *Xiánhúán* (銜環): See above. ○
The Great Learning says: "Wealth enriches the house; virtue enriches the person. [The section on] "Capable of Governing the Family" is seen above.
Regarding merchants, the *Baihūtong* says: "One who dwells selling is called a *jiǎ* (merchant); one who circulates goods is called a *shāng* (trader).
"Those who produce act with haste; those who use act with ease. The ways of generating wealth are found together in the *Daxue*.
Having encountered wind and waves, the merchant returns to fulfill his vow;
floating upon the boundless river, he laments the shared peril of the traveler’s boat. With a karmic affinity, Fǎhǎi has ascended and gained passage upon the raft of the Way.
I respectfully select an auspicious morning to repay this great kindness. I, [Name], reflect deeply that my resolve is earnest and my plans profound, seeking to complete the ancestral hall.
While enriching one's household, I was preoccupied with the pursuit of petty profits, until suddenly I was startled by the perils of the whale-waves.

This wretched illusory body nearly met its end in the belly of a river fish, and these abundant treasures were on the verge of sinking into the abyss of the dragon-infested deep. Thereupon, I knocked at the gate of the Honored One, the Tamer of Men.
Thus, one is spared from the suffering of drifting and drowning; such kindness is rare indeed. What do you think?

(Entering the Buddhist ritual) We humbly pray that the source of benefit may overflow and the ocean of merit remain deep and still. In every movement and station, may we forever encounter the protection of Mañjuśrī;
in every transaction, may we find our place and meet with the auspiciousness of the Joyful Treasury.
“Lun xu” (mutually perishing) and “gu dan” (at dawn) appear above. “Ken tang” (able to fill the hall) and “run wu” (moistening the house) appear together above.

Regarding “miao miao” (tiny/microscopic), the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian), “Basic Annals of Shiwu,” states: “I, with my microscopic body, have inherited the supreme honor; I am apprehensive and fearful that I may not be equal to the task.
Regarding “the belly of a river fish,” this appears in Qu Yuan’s “The Fisherman. “Yang yi” (overflowing) appears in the middle [section].

Yong. Furthermore, when encountering wind and waves, I offered my sincere prayers to Feilian, the wind atop the surging billows. My Buddha appeared like the moon reflected in the water, and my wish was immediately fulfilled.

Moved by this resonance, I have laid bare my sincere heart to repay your vast protection. I reflect deeply that I, [Name], am but a lowly personage like a blade of grass, with a drifting life like a floating weed.
My return home has been like crossing the Yangtze River; I have drifted and fallen as if dwelling upon the great ocean.

The howling winds and battling rains were like thunder from the land of grace, while the sun-drenching clouds and swallowing mists turned into snow that obscures the heavens. I wish to escape the dragon’s abyss.
In this time of difficulty, we invoke the venerable Ni-zuo; truly relying upon his vast compassion, we immediately receive auspicious guidance.

Aspiring to form a thatched hut, we shall emulate the sunflower’s inclination toward the light. (Entering for the Buddhist ceremony) We pray that coin shall flow upon the ground and goods abound at midday.
May jade be piled and pearls fill the store, so that the very gateway becomes a marketplace; may rivers swell and clouds gather, rendering unnecessary the frequent climbing of monopolistic mounds.
○Fei Lian (Flying Licorice) ○Di Ji (Following Auspiciousness) ○Cao Jie (Grass Knots) ○Kui Qing (Hemp-Leaf Inclination)—all are seen above.

○Qian Liu Di Shang Qian Dai Shi (Coins Flow on the Ground; Former Loans of Food). The *Zhuan* says: "Therefore, goods and treasures were valued in gold, their utility was in knives, and they flowed like springs.
The commentary by Ru Chun says: "The reason money is called 'knives' is because it is beneficial to the people; furthermore, it circulates like a spring."
Furthermore, the *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* says: "At midday, the market is held;
the people of the world are brought there, and the goods of the world are gathered. They trade with one another and then depart, each obtaining what they require.
Regarding monopolies, Mencius said: "There is a base fellow who must seek out a monopoly and climb upon it, looking left and right to ensnare [the people]."
"City profits. The commentary states: "Those who look left and right desire to obtain this while also taking that. "Entangling net" (*wang*) refers to capturing them with a net.
A wife who acts as a merchant for her husband and does not return establishes a vow.

I reflect that my husband has long been a traveler without a home; I, his wife at this frontier of Jing, respectfully exhaust my sincere devotion and establish a solemn covenant to reverently perform Buddhist rites.
I earnestly consider how my husband, [Name], for the sake of profit like that of a leather bag, traveled far as a son on a long journey.
As days passed and months went by, I had no knowledge of his whereabouts; enduring wind and rain while eating and sleeping, how could I bear such toil as a woman with feet like silkworm cocoons?

The toil of this [separation]—he dwells at the edge of heaven, while I reside in a corner of the earth. Having not yet attained the joy of turning the chariot back, I can only deepen my longing as I raise the dining tray.
With bowed head I pray for grace, and with a sincere heart I take refuge. (Enter into Buddhist rites.

I humbly pray that [Name] may stir the sentiments of Yuanming regarding the pines and chrysanthemums, and arouse Zhang Han’s thoughts of the water-celery and drumfish. Without lingering or dwelling, let him proceed upon the tracks of rest.
Amidst the vicissitudes of our parting, may your words of returning and coming home fulfill the covenant of meeting at the edge of the blade.

Regarding the phrase "Gao-zhen" (the one who grinds the straw), an ancient *yuefu* poem asks: "Where is Gao-zhen now? Upon the mountain there is yet another mountain. The commentary notes that "Gao-zhen" is a metaphor for the husband.
By asking where the husband is on the mountain—and since "mountain" (*shan*) is a homophone for the character "out" (*chū*)—it signifies that the husband has gone abroad.
The *Biography of the Archivist Fan Li* states: "Fan Li sailed across the sea to Qi, where he changed his name and styled himself 'Chiyi Zizi' (the Leather Bag Son).
He farmed by the seashore. The *Suoyin* commentary notes: "This is what Fan Li called himself.
It is likely because the King of Wu had killed Zi Xu and placed him in a leather bag (*chīyí*); now, Fan Li, considering himself guilty of similar faults, [adopted this name]."
This is a title. Wei Zhao said: "Chiyi" refers to a leather bag; others say it is raw cowhide.
○ "The days pass and the months advance" is seen in the *Xiaowan* (Small Ostrich) of the *Shijing*. ○ "Callused feet" means that the skin on the feet has become thick and heavy.
When the state of Chu intended to attack Song, Mozi traveled from Lu to Chu; for ten days and ten nights his feet swelled like heavy cocoons, yet he did not stop.

*Sī* (Sore): This refers to the skin of the feet being wounded and peeling like a thick cocoon. *Tianya* (End of Heaven) and *Dijiao* (Corner of Earth): In Wu Rong’s *Jin Shanshui Ge* (Song of Exhausting Mountains and Waters), it says:
"The corner of the earth is brought within a square inch; the end of heaven is written upon the tip of the brush. *Ju'an* (Raising the Tray):
The *Lie Nü Zhuan* (Biographies of Exemplary Women) states: Meng Guang, whose courtesy name was Deyao, had many neighbors seeking a match for her, yet [her father] would not choose one.
She was given in marriage. When her parents asked the reason for this, Guang said, "I wish to find a man as virtuous as Liang Boluan.

When Li Hong heard of this, he went to marry her. Upon her arrival at the gate, she was adorned with finery; however, after seven days, Hong gave no response. Guang said, "The attire of a concubine is the dress of one in seclusion.
Hong rejoiced and said, "This is truly the wife of Liang Hong. Later, being poor, they took up work by hire and entered Bailong Mountain.

Those in the central region took agriculture and sericulture as their occupations. Whenever Guang presented food to Hong, she would always hold the table level with her eyebrows, not daring to look up at him.
○ Regarding "Pines and Chrysanthemums," see Huan Yuanming’s *Guiqulai Ci* (Return of the Wild Duck). ○ Regarding "Duckweed and Minnows," Zhang Han: his courtesy name was Jiying.
He possessed refined talent and was skilled in composing literature. During the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, he served under Prince Qian of Qi.
He was appointed as a clerk in the Eastern Office (*dōngcáo*). When the autumn winds arose, he longed for the water-millet greens and duckweed soup of Wu, and the sliced raw fish of the Shǐ River.

He sighed, saying, "In human life, one merely seeks the fulfillment of one's will; what is the use of wealth and honor? He then took his leave and departed. After many hardships, he had an audience with the Emperor.
"Upon the hilt of the sword" (*dāotóu*) is an ancient *yùefǔ* (ballad). It asks: "When shall the great sword-hilt / And the broken mirror fly up to heaven?"

The commentary states: As for the period of return, it is measured by the month; it is like the ring found on the hilt of a sword when the mirror is broken. Therefore it says: "Because of litigation, one prays for peace;
through mutual discord, one has already become ashamed before the Immortal of Forbearance. That both fortune and misfortune are clearly revealed truly relies upon the Buddha who bestows compassion."

I respectfully submit this to Your Imperial Enlightenment and humbly offer my sincere devotion. I reflect deeply that throughout my life I have endured hardship and toil, and I have always stood in awe of the three-foot ruler of the law.
Lately, however, due to a breach with an enemy, I have suddenly been embroiled in the beginnings of a legal dispute; the threat of being reduced to a wooden effigy is truly my greatest anxiety.
In whose judgment can we rely upon the shade of the *Gāngtáng* tree? I seek only the auspiciousness of the center, yet I am deeply apprehensive of ultimate calamity.

I do not dare hope for your compassionate benevolence to grant me peace and tranquility. (Entering the ritual) I prostrate myself with the vow that the clouds of compassion may cover and protect us, and the sun of wisdom may shine its light.

There is nothing obscure that you do not perceive, and no wish that remains unfulfilled. It is only I who have made this request; whatever is unjust shall surely be rectified, and whatever is doubtful shall surely be resolved. It rests with me...
There is no interruption.
○ The Immortal of Patience (Kṣāntivādin) saw the *Dazang yilan* (Comprehensive Survey of the Great Canon). ○ Regarding the vow to carve wood, the *Wenshu zhuan* (Biography of Wen Shu) says:

When this wisdom is attained, one accepts and maintains the principle that all dharmas are non-arising; it is certain and without error. Because the object and the wisdom are in perfect accord, it is called the patience of non-arising.

On the essence and the soul (*jingpo*), as well as the leaves of the *xie* plant, see the previous section. Regarding the wind moving the branches of trees, the *Han Shi Waizhuan* says:
When Confucius was traveling abroad, he heard a cry of profound sorrow. Upon arriving there, it was Gao Yu.
Wearing coarse cloth and clutching his sword, he wept on the left side of the road. Confucius alighted from his carriage and asked him the reason for his grief.
He replied, "In my youth, I was fond of learning and traveled throughout the world, yet my parents passed away; this was my first failure.

Later, I held my aspirations high and would not serve mediocre lords, yet I achieved nothing in my later years; this was my second failure. In my youth, I lost my circle of companions and became sparse in close friends."
To grow old without anyone to rely upon is the third loss. Now, one may wish for the trees to be still, yet the wind does not cease;
one may wish to nourish one’s parents, yet it is too late. That which passes and cannot be returned is age; that which departs and cannot be pursued is one’s parents.
"I shall therefore take my leave. He stood weeping and died right there. Thirteen disciples of Confucius returned home to care for their parents.
"I have no leisure to sit or rest" is seen in the poem "The Four Horses" (*Sishou*).

Therefore, a *dōjō* (sacred precinct) is established to provide spiritual sustenance for the path to the netherworld. I reflect with deep sorrow upon my late father, [Name], whose labors were arduous and whose virtue was profound, who nurtured and educated me...
The grace bestowed is profound. Formerly, in a dream, the yellow bear suddenly entered the realm where all traces vanish and all sounds cease;

now, the white horse is enshrined, fortunately relying upon this land where souls are gathered and spirits are concealed. Thus, we repay the boundless kindness of our ancestors and respectfully follow the rites of Great Compassion.
(Entering the Buddhist service) We humbly pray that our late lord [Name] may behold his pure body amidst the mountain scenery and hear the broad and long tongue [of the Buddha].
Within the sound of the mountain stream, one’s original face is suddenly encountered; the life-root of beginningless time is instantly severed with a snap.
Regarding death, it is as recorded in the *Tán Gōng*: "At the onset of death, the body swells up as if it were about to burst.

it was truly enshrined in the suburban sacrifice of Xia, and the three dynasties thereafter continued to worship it.

Since Jin served as the hegemon, perhaps they had failed to perform this sacrifice. When the Marquis of Jin performed the suburban sacrifice of Xia, his illness subsided, and he bestowed [a fief] upon Zichan.
He produced two square tripods inscribed with "Sanju" (Produced at Sanju). Fan Shi, styled Jujing, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Baima.

I have changed into the mourning attire appropriate for a friend and hastened here to attend the funeral. Yet before I arrived, the funeral procession had already departed."
When they had reached the grave pit and were about to lower the coffin, it refused to move forward. His mother patted it and said, "Yuanbo, do you have some lingering hope?
She then halted the coffin for a long while, whereupon she saw a white carriage and a white horse approaching. The mother said, "This must be Juqing.
She then took hold of the ropes and pulled; the coffin then moved forward. ○ The debt of infinite kindness.

Suddenly all obstructions were cleared away like ice melting and snow dissolving; beneath the shimmering lattice of jewel nets, one pays homage to the Compassionate Honored One;
amidst the ethereal drifting of celestial flowers, one hears the wondrous music.
Regarding the kinship of the *qiáo* tree, the *Shuōwén Jì* states: When Bóqīn and Kāngshū visited the Duke of Wǔ (Zhōu Gōng), they were flogged three times upon their third visit.
They then questioned Shāng Zǐ, who said, "On the southern slope of the South Mountain there is a tree named *qiáo*;

the catalpa represents the way of the son. (Note: As a son, when seeing his father, if he cannot humble himself and be submissive and compliant like the catalpa tree which is full yet bows downward, he will therefore suffer a flogging. [Section on Changing Places] "Deep Spring" is both seen above.

yet, failing to fulfill the filial debt of three springs, I wish to deliver her from the sufferings of the netherworld and thus appeal to the Buddha’s compassion. I humbly reflect that my deceased mother, [Name], while respectfully residing in the northern hall, was diligent in her duties.

[The account of] the Twin Sāla Trees is above. Regarding the First Patriarch Bodhidharma of the Congling Mountains:

he sat at Shaolin for nine years and first transmitted the Dharma and the *kāṣāya* to Huìkè. He then resided at Qiānshèng Temple on Mount Yǔmén. On the fifth day of the tenth month, he passed away while sitting upright.

Days pass like years; hunger parches the throat and blurred vision clouds the eyes. Your gaunt bones stand out in stark relief, your form like a withered tree.
To whom can you tell of such sorrow? In this state, it is difficult to apply any expedient means.

Fortunately, tonight the host of this vegetarian feast, [Name], has specifically invited monks to his home for [specific purpose], opening wide the gate of liberation and inaugurating a gathering of relief. You all should...
It is best to reflect upon yourself; do not wait for others to examine you. When encountering enemies, let each person find their own release;
when hearing the sublime Dharma, let everyone rejoice together. Mind is Buddha, and Buddha is mind; simply turn the light back to reflect within yourself.
Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; do not mistake the false for the true. Thus I post this notice.
A Notice for the Offering of Alms:
It is said that all human beings possess the Buddha-nature. Its radiance is limitless, far surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon;
it is vast and ineffable, exceeding the dimensions of empty space. Alas, how one chases after external objects and suddenly loses this [nature] of one's own accord!
Household treasures [are but illusions]. The transgressions of the six thieves deepen further; the sufferings of the three paths grow ever more severe. What is the nature of karmic conditions?
If one recognizes them for what they are, they are immediately resolved. Retributive obstacles are fundamentally empty; yet when deluded, they remain unavoidable throughout kalpas.
Fortunately, tonight the host of this vegetarian feast (Name), for the sake of (specific matter), has invited Bhikṣus to offer a meal of *sū-dhā*. Since you have all come to attend—
Gathering: You must all be solemn and reverent in your three karmas, upright and attentive in your single mind. Repent for past errors and seek the rightness of today.
The "soup of wood shavings" and "rice with iron nails" are precisely what you should attend to; the "cloud-gate cakes" and "Zhaozhou tea" require only the opening of the mouth.
Should you violate these precepts and covenants, you will only increase your own sinking into samsara. You create this difficulty yourself—whose fault is it? Therefore, this notice is posted.
Furthermore, I lament for you, sons of the Buddha, who have fallen into this dark path. These instruments of suffering are certainly not of a single kind; they all arise from your own actions.

How could the weight of this sorrow be fully recounted? It is by no means the work of another. It is simply because of a single thought of greed or anger that you have thus experienced such afflictions throughout successive lives.

Since you already know that your past was mistaken and erroneous, why must you beat your breast and stamp your feet? If you wish to attain immediate liberation, you must urgently change your strings and alter your course.
Tonight, the host [Name] has prepared this *hūi* (offering of food) for [specific purpose]. Now, meeting with this auspicious assembly, one must receive its sublime guidance.
The nature of sin is fundamentally empty—what more is there to do or to undergo? Delusive conditions are not real; it is just like...
Illusion arises and illusion perishes. If one can awaken to and enter into the single mind, one may overturn the nine stages of realization.
If you violate these clear instructions, how will you escape the wheel of suffering? Do not persist in your former errors; maintain right mindfulness. Thus, this notice is posted.

The *Tongzai* (Comprehensive Record) of the Tiantai Zhi says: The Tiantai Master Zhi, whose name was Zhigyi, style name De’an, surnamed Chen, was a native of Yingchuan.
He went to Mount Daisu in Guangzhou to receive instruction in the mental contemplation (*xin-guan*) from Master Nan Yue.
Thereupon, he practiced the *Lotus Samādhi* on the northern mountain; after staying there for only three nights, he reached the "Medicine King" chapter while reciting the sutra.
The mind taking suffering as its object is the true phrase for diligent effort (*vīrya*). Upon attaining understanding, realization suddenly arose:
he saw himself together with his teacher on Vulture Peak, in a pure land of the seven treasures, listening to the Buddha preach the Dharma. He took this vision as a seal of approval.

Later, the Master personally led the Chan community in performing the *Guangming* Repentance. This was in accordance with the teachings of the Master of Repentance Ciyun, the Dharma Master Ciyun of India.
Shi (style name Zhibai), surnamed Ye, was a native of Ninghai, Tiantai. His mother, Lady Wang, dreamed of swallowing a bright pearl before giving birth to him.
When he grew older, he took no pleasure in following his elder brother in trade; he went secretly to Dongye Mountain to enter the monastic life.
At the age of twenty, he went to Chenlin to receive full ordination. The following year, he studied the Vinaya under Shouchu. Shi subsequently entered Guoqing Pusa Temple.
Before the image of the Venerable One, he burned off a finger as a vow to transmit the teachings of Tiantai.

The gates of the Bodhimanda join with the pavilions as the auspicious signs of heaven unfold extensively; they follow freely beneath the lion throne.
Banners and flowers intermingle as the Buddha’s light radiates afar toward Vulture Peak;
when the rain of Dharma falls, the mundane world is now entirely a pure land.
Wherever the Buddha’s light descends, what is not the Western Paradise within this very site of enlightenment?
The gateless gate is the very gate of liberation; whether north, south, east, or west, one need only recognize the starting point and the way of entry.
That which is not the mind is the Buddha of one’s own mind; gods, humans, ghosts, and animals all come to breathe through the same nostril.
At the guest-hall on the journey through heaven and earth, I sit watching how many travelers come and go;
in the passage of spring and autumn, I am startled by the turning of the grindstone of human life— how many have already returned?
Having thoroughly investigated and severed the mind of permanence and annihilation, let it be that for a hundred years everything is but a dream.
Having fully understood the affairs of arising and ceasing, look upon this world as being entirely like a bubble.
How many such illusions and dreams! Outside the gate, white clouds arise and vanish again.
The Zen mind dwells nowhere; like the bright moon atop the peak, it departs and returns.
To fully realize that the nature of awakening is beyond coming and going is to manifest extinction and return to primordial quiescence.
Having scrutinized and penetrated Jambudvīpa as entirely illusory and transformative, one casts off birth and realizes non-birth. (The above is for use by monks.)
The *chun* tree suddenly withers, yet its *zhi* sprouts appear in pairs as they return to Great Enlightenment;
the lotus flowers flourish in full bloom, each blossom in the golden channel manifesting the entire body. (Father:

Sorrowful clouds fill the courtyard, causing the cassia seeds to feel profound grief.
(By Father Yong of Autumn) Having no way to play with colorful silks, the silent hall of motherwort turns into a night dream.
Choosing a neighbor, what can one rely on as the autumn wind stirs the fragrant orchards?
(Mother) The bitter taste of bear gall is hard to forget; I listen with sorrow as the cuckoo cries under the night moon.
The sound of the loom’s thread momentarily ceases; I cannot bear to watch the tender wood move in the spring breeze. (Mother)
With hair tied up, my feelings have become empty and my hopes severed; the returning clouds leave behind but a stone.
The matter of painted brows is now a parting; when dreams return, I find only an empty pavilion where I used to worship the moon. (The husband has gone abroad and the wife has passed away.
Though the love for the calf is difficult to extinguish, facing these scenes, my grieving heart is ever more pained.
The fragrance of the books in the chest has just dissipated—a place that wounds the heart; the blood-cry of the crane is endless.
(Son) Mount Tai suddenly collapses, and ten thousand ravines wail; clouds add to the sorrow of parting.
From the eastern bedchamber comes a sigh, as for a thousand autumns dark rains continue the sound of separation. (Father-in-law)
The Buddha-sun shines upon the jade casket, its hundred treasures radiating auspicious colors;
sandalwood smoke enshrouds the lunar form, while auspicious clouds swirl around the thousand-flower pedestal.
The essence of the five classes of *tāla* leaves is fundamentally empty; though translated to the very bottom, not a single word remains.
All merits are inherently complete within one's own mind; when the entire body is pressed into this state, a thousand auspicious signs arise.
(End of Sūtra) For those who awaken to and enter the Flower Treasury Adornment, which is equal to the great void, the three bodies are perfectly manifested.
The thunderous sound vibrates universally throughout the sand-grains of the world-realms; wherever it is heard, the four virtues are fully manifested.
Gazing upon the flower-seat and prostrating before the compassionate countenance, one must encounter his true face.
Striking the golden bell and chanting the *brahman* hymns, may you not let the faculty of "hearing the reverse" remain obscured.
May the Dharma rain enter the *xuan* forest, and the spring colors reflect upon the brocade of the magnificent hall.
May the breeze of compassion waft over the cassia blossoms, and the celestial fragrance join the lotuses of the azure pond. (For the child to cultivate merit for the mother.)
If one were to rely on the fundamental reality, which does not involve cultivation or achievement, what need would there be for reciting sutras or prostrating to the Buddha?
To accommodate the needs of the present age, surely there must be expedient means; it is precisely here that one should properly offer water and flowers.
When the gate of non-duality opens for the assembly to enter together, the sky is vast and the sea is wide;
when the path leading back home is cleared for all to travel together, the sun is warm and the breeze is gentle.
Auspicious vapors embrace the Southern Mountains on the occasion of His Majesty’s longevity; a single *tánhuā* blooms within the realm of long life.
Auspicious clouds support the morning sun as thousand-year-old dark cranes dance through the glorious season.

The spiritual resonance of paying homage to the thousand Buddhas is inconceivable; throughout the three periods of time, they are not separate from the present thought-moment. To speak further, it is as if meeting them yet not meeting them.

Their coming and going leave no trace, yet they manifest simultaneously within a single hair-tip throughout the ten directions. One must simply forget both the one who pays homage and the object of homage.
On the night of the first day of the New Year, when the lanterns of a thousand gates shine with radiant beauty, the Tathāgata of Blazing Radiance extends his solitary hand;
where the spring splendor of silk and brocade fills ten li, the Bodhisattva of Great Adornment reveals his entire body.
In the nine thoroughfares, the sounds of pipes and songs fill the springtime as all celebrate the era of Great Harmony;
in a thousand homes, the lights and fires shine like a thousand moons as they eternally rejoice in this world of No-Night.
The Mid-Autumn Festival.
Gathering the power of the Saṃgha to repay the kindness of one’s parents is like rejoicing in the brilliance of a thousand lamps within a dark chamber;
relying on the Buddha’s compassion to practice the methods of repentance is like bringing back the spring of ten thousand kalpas to a cold cliff.
Who among us has no kin? Whether man or woman, let everyone together resolve their will.
Who is not a Buddha? Bearing the same name and title, you shall surely receive your prediction of enlightenment all at once. (The assembly:
We have fully fulfilled the mother’s vegetarian feast.
In the Forest of Merit, the day-lilies (*xuancao*) display the splendor of eternal spring;
within the Blood Basin Pond, lotuses bloom with an unceasing fragrance.
In the Huayan Hall, the sutras are intoned.
One must know that the eighty-one fascicles of the True Commentary are inherently complete from the very beginning.
It is not an obstacle for the fifty-three patriarchs to directly participate together; this is for the purpose of commemorating the deceased.
Contemplating the fundamental emptiness of the nature of transgressions, one drains the great ocean to reveal a golden land;
realizing that the Pure Land is not far away, one spans the void to construct an iron bridge.
Just as the nectar of immortality begins to moisten, the flower-wheel suddenly unfolds in five colors.
The Dharma-thunder roars suddenly, directly shattering the thousand-fold iron mesh;
before the mirror of karma, a single stroke of spring wind blows away the lingering mists.
Within the realm of Yama, the rain of the Threefold Dharma washes away the turbid dust. (Fiftieth Stanza)
The place of delusion is a dark recess that requires the torch for piercing the darkness;
once awakening is attained, it becomes a pure land—what need is there for a boat to enter purity? (Sixty characters) Bathing the Buddha.
The Buddha-body is unborn, yet it delivers beings of the six realms according to their capacities; only then does one realize that its wondrous skillful means are unfathomable.

How could the Dharma-body be defiled? Yet, when it manifests transformation, it washes away the defilements of the myriad spirits, so that the profound grace of initial awakening constantly nourishes all.
On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment,
six years of arduous toil had finally revealed that there was nothing at all;
in a single morning he saw it through and regretted having spent so much time on the Snowy Peaks.
In praying for male descendants, the ancestors have maintained the sacrificial rites for a hundred generations; were it not for seeking a son like Zhèn, how could these rites be continued?
In the Buddha’s wondrous response to the two arrivals, one hopes that by managing the household affairs, the family can finally be revitalized.
Having prayed for good fortune, I rejoice at holding the single pearl in the palm of my hand;
with many auspicious signs upon the hearth, I further hope that the three phoenixes shall dance before the courtyard.
May official affairs be preserved.
In failing to exercise caution in my affairs, I am already ashamed that my resolve has fallen short of the covenant carved upon wood.
Though my sincerity is now obstructed, I only pray to borrow the shade of the *gan-tang* tree;
for these initial words, I truly offer them merely as a testament to this obstruction of sincerity.
In the midst of these matters, you encounter good fortune; may you wish for eternal peace and the blessing of freedom from litigation.
(Vow-fulfillment prayer) When merchants travel abroad, they first think of the benefit of crossing rivers via flowing springs.
Gathering goods at midday, one hopes only for the successful completion of the journey to the burial mound.
As officials depart for their posts, may travelers on the road be secure from peril; may auspicious clouds follow the sun across ten thousand li.
In the government offices, there is much celebration as the grace of the Nine Heavens has been bestowed in a timely drenching.
We offer thanks for the rain; we gaze longingly, fearing it will dry up, having long suffered under the blinding glare of the crimson wheels of official carriages.
The shimmering scales of the clouds arise as one joyfully beholds the hanging silver bamboos;
yet, to ward off fire by embracing it before it has even ignited is truly a matter of immediate concern for one’s neighbor.
Encountering disaster and knowing fear, one may first implement the defenses of the ancient earthworks;
within the period of a single retreat, one seizes the pearl from atop the topknot, being truly capable of transforming the mundane and forging the sacred.
Among the fourfold assembly, the moon atop the platform will surely reflect upon the earth and shine upon the heavens;
it shall flow as an ocean of merit into the realm of non-being, so that even the blades of grass shall be moistened by the transformative rain.
Establishing the banner of radiance within the inconceivable realm, even those in secluded crags alike receive the compassionate glow.

When chanting the sutras, the standard practice is to begin with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*); yet, by first striking out this preceding phrase and overturning it, one causes even the lanterns to be illuminated.
The pillar reveals its forehead and raises its brows; which sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood?
Having received and practiced this with faith, there remains one final barrier at the end:
if you can pass through this barrier, let even curd and milk form rivers and gold turn the earth—whose Pure Land would not then be nothing but mind?
In the seven-foot room, a withered vine leans toward the clouds beyond; A single lamp hangs the ancestral flame.
With a single branch of a decayed whisk, one sweeps amidst the moonlight; On half a mat, one lies through the autumn wind.
For long I have donned a single *kaṣāya* robe, gazing with indifference upon the streams and mountains; who cares whether the clouds unfurl or curl?
I merely hold my prayer beads to pass the years and months; who knows that flowers fall and bloom?
— Guest Hall.
When meeting, one must look into the mirror before the pivot; only upon arrival does one know the mystery beyond the norm.
In the Hall of the Ten Directions, the Buddha-dharma is like a great forge and red furnace: whatever is iron is fit to be cast.
A Zen monk is like a solitary cloud or a wild crane; to what heaven cannot he fly?
When the objects within the Buddha Hall are arrayed as adornments, they are themselves the transcendence of adornment; at that very moment, one ascends to the precious abode.
Splitting asunder the void to manifest the marks and signs—yet these are not marks and signs—is what is called "marks and signs. When they appear before one, the Tathāgata is seen instantaneously.
The ocean of boundless vows merges with hundreds of thousands of fragrant waters, yet its depth remains beyond comparison; thus, all nine realms universally partake in the holy grace.
The Hall of Pure Deeds, where the banner of inexhaustible radiance outshines the illumination of ten billion suns and moons, such that its compassionate brilliance illuminates all ten directions.
Only when a single thought is suddenly empty can it be said that Amitābha appears;
only when all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent should one know that my Pure Land is fully manifest.
Avalokiteśvara Pavilion.
Truly contemplating that wherever suffering arises, it is fundamentally empty from the beginning—this is called the power of mastery, constantly rescuing those in distress.
When the Right Dharma shines forth, sentient beings have long since attained Buddhahood; this is the realization of the practice of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha) in every place.
Benefiting sentient beings:
the moon peering through the window reveals the colors of the pines, all of which manifest the true Prajñā;
the wind sounding before the railing carries the voices of the bamboos, every sound entering the Great Perfect Penetration.
At the three gates, heavenly flowers rain down amidst the verdant peaks; if you smell them, you must be most careful.
Upon the ground, golden cords lie within the azure mists; as you walk along, do not hesitate for a moment.
Do not suspect the ways of the world; drifting clouds rest upon the setting sun at the temple gate.
If you can seek the mechanism of Chan, the bright moon in the stream carries a solitary sail.
Ancestral Hall.
Before the courtyard of Shaoshi, a thousand fathoms of white clouds stand cold;
amidst the yellow plum blossoms, a single wheel of bright moon transmits the robe at night.
The Monastery Hall.
Through the wondrous skillful means of permitting and prohibiting, you directly cause the monastic community to return to the realm of awakening;
through numerous expedients of compliance and resistance, you secretly support the holy transformation so that it permeates the mundane world.
[The Veda Temple...]
Secretly employing divine power, you open the path to enlightenment; practicing compassion and patience in reverse order, you protect the monastic grove.
If the five contemplations in the cloud-hall are as clear as refined gold, they will transform easily; when drinking tea, one must recognize that within the tea there is bone.
If the three poisons of the mind are not resolved, water cannot be digested; when eating rice, one must find the husks within it.

We humbly submit that the cycles of the *zhengyuan* (the fundamental principle) shift; how constant can the configurations of antiquity and the present ever be? The division of Heaven and Earth manifests the designations of "above" and "below."
Our original resolve is firm; our humble hearts possess an indestructible principle. In the Great Changes (*Da Yi*), there is the calamity of "unfounded suspicion.

Desiring to manifest our slight loyalty like that of dogs and horses, we briefly set forth our meager sincerity like that of ants and bees. We, [Your Subjects] (Name), with utmost humility and trepidation, prostrate ourselves and address Your Majesty:
We humbly consider that within this realm, the Three Great Ones are most venerated, and how could we dare forget the heart of offering reverence? Even the Buddhist scriptures...
I revere the four debts of gratitude and harbor a profound sense of duty to repay their kindness. Whether it be insects that crawl or creatures that fly, who could turn their backs on transformation?

Under the sun and sky, even the grass by the stream and the flowers upon the crags are all moistened by the gentle breeze and sweet rain. Throughout the heavens, all are granted clemency; wherever one goes, one returns to benevolence.
This is because we humbly encounter Your Majesty, the Emperor, whose divine intelligence is bestowed from Heaven and whose heroic prowess is innate. You regard the people as if they were wounded.
He emulated the supreme virtue of King Wen of Zhou by regulating his own person through frugality, matching the grand plan of Yu of Xia.

Yet, as the fortunes of the state were declining, celestial calamities consequently arrived one after another; amidst hundreds of thousands of changes, the burden of toil and anxiety fell solely upon the One Man.

Seventeen years of toil and anxiety could not have been relieved in even half a day. We suffer the calamity of the "Nine Suns" (the ultimate disaster), and endure the misfortune of the "Dragon's Excess" (the drought of tyranny).

Disaster arises from the shallow ponds as rebel traitors spread their nets of gold; the mechanism is deep-seated like a rat in the shrine, as a rebellious eunuch opens the door for his own decapitation.
This causes the Dragon Carriage to ascend suddenly, abandoning the myriad affairs of state without a backward glance, while the countenance of Heaven grows ever more...
How desolate! We mourn that the nine regions of the earth have no place of reliance. We, [Name] and others, are lowly ones clad in field-weeds, shaven-headed remnants of the people.
Stupid and ignorant, what do we know? Having left the secular world, we are content to be like wild deer; living in poverty and cold, surviving by mere chance, we are truly like drifting tumbleweeds.

Borrowing the moisture of the waves of grace, we feel ashamed that our slightest virtue offers no contribution. Seeking to prolong our lives in the grassy wilds, how can we find a way to redeem ourselves a hundredfold? In vain...
There exists the classification of the *Fan* and *Zhu* [Sanskrit and Chinese] traditions; we have exhausted our devotion as members of the monastic community (*saṃgha*).

Relying above upon the vast vows of the Buddha and the Devas, and gathering below the refined sincerity of the monks' conduct, we have diligently performed the *Lianghuang Chánfǎ* (Repentance Ritual of Emperor Liang) for seven days and secretly practiced the *yogācāra* of the Ancient Buddhas at midnight.
By means of these roots of goodness, we reverently adorn the Imperial Personage. We humbly pray that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue may flourish daily.
The Tianxi era has flourished even more greatly. Your spirit roams the Golden Gate, returning to illuminate the Buddha-sun across the various heavens;

you nurture virtue upon the Lotus Terrace, while continuing to spread imperial benevolence throughout the nine realms. We pray once again that you will not withhold the light of your favor, and that you will bestow the auspiciousness of averting misfortune and ending decline.

The malevolent spirits have been swept away, and the universe once again beholds tranquility and peace. We silently consolidate the imperial domain, all rejoicing in the eternal covenant of mountains and rivers.

Heaven collapses and earth cracks, with deep agony piercing straight through to the crimson heart. In vain one harbors the sorrowful sincerity of a blade of grass, unable to repay the great transformation of the three springs.
Thus, following the legacy of the ancient sovereigns, I specifically proffer the reverence of the "tiger-kowtow," and repeatedly invoke the sublime names of the Sugata.

Exhausting my sincerity with cries of "Long Live" like those from Mount Song, I uphold the secret seals of Yoga; raining down the wealth of the Dharma from the midst of space, I manifest the wondrous radiance of *Hrīḥ* to shatter the iron city beneath the earth.
By cultivating this minute merit, even as small as a pinch of grain, I look upward to repay the vast grace of the Great Chaos.
I humbly pray that the heavenly mandate may flourish ever more, the Imperial residence remain secure, and the divine majesty spread far and wide to bring about a new era of peace.
The mountains and rivers of this realm have been restored; Your Majesty’s sagely virtue flourishes ever more, once again raising high the sun and moon of great brilliance.

You have turned back the destiny of slaughter and elevated the common people to a heaven of benevolence and longevity. Having utterly extinguished the demonic miasma, you have transformed the great mechanism of the cosmos into a realm of purity and tranquility.
(I, [Name]), unable to restrain my most fervent and earnest supplications, respectfully submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal.
Regarding "Relying on the Protectors," the sincerity with which one performs the *yue* sacrifice is as explained above. Regarding the "Four Reliances," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka* states:
first, wearing rag robes; second, constantly practicing alms-gathering; third, sitting at the foot of a tree; and fourth, using stale and decayed medicine. The "Six Articles" refer to:
first, robes; second, an alms bowl; third, a sitting mat; fourth, a paper blanket; and fifth, a whisk. (The sixth is a water filter.)
Sixth, the Hand-held Incense Burner. ○ Regarding "the stubborn metal that leaps from the furnace," see above.

In the fourth year of the Tianfeng era, the year Dingchou (47 CE), Wang Mang’s nature was volatile and agitated, and his laws and regulations were vexatious and oppressive.

Labor services were burdensome and frequent, while droughts and locust plagues followed one after another. Legal cases remained unresolved, and officials took advantage of the situation to exploit and oppress the people.
The wealthy could not protect their property, and the poor had no means of survival; consequently, they rose up together as bandits. Among them was Wang Kuang, a native of Xinsi in Jingzhou.
Wang Feng, Ma Wu of Nanyang, and Wang Chang and Cheng Dan of Yingchuan gathered together to take refuge in Mount Lülín, where their numbers reached eight thousand.
When Xuanyuan ascended to heaven, he appeared before the Emperor. Regarding the passing of Fuxun, the *Shun Dian* states:
"In the twenty-eighth year, the Emperor then passed away. The commentary notes that "cúluò" (徂落) means death.
"Lonely Indignation": Lu Ji’s *Treatise on the Refutation of Defeat* states: "Though loyal ministers harbor lonely indignation and ranked officers offer up their lives, what can they possibly save?
"The White Rainbow Pierces the Bright Sun": The *Biography of Jing Ke* in the *Records of the Grand Historian* states:

When Jing Ke plotted for the Crown Prince of Yan to assassinate the King of Qin, at that time a white rainbow pierced the bright sun. "Inch of Grass, Three Springs": This is seen in [the writings of] San Chun.

Regarding "At the top": *Huibai shijiangan* (The Tiger’s Prostration at the Poem on the Yangtze and Han Rivers) states: "The tiger prostrates with his head to the ground. The commentary says: "Tiger" is the courtesy name of Duke Mu.
Regarding "Sung hu" (Crying out to Song): see above. Regarding "Guicuo" (A pinch and a spoonful):

the *Lilishi zhi* (Annals of Music and Calendar) states: "Not missing even a pinch or a spoonful. The commentary says: Ying Shao notes that the "gui" (pinch) is a natural form, the beginning of Yin and Yang; four "gui" make one "cuo" (spoonful).
Pinch it with three fingers. ○ [This] was presented to the Emperor during the Qingning era.

Having heard that the rebel forces were rampant, the Dharma-transmitting Abbot Bhikṣu (Name) of Yongquan Chan Monastery at Gushan respectfully selects the first day of the third month of this year to recite sutras and submit a memorial for the protection of the state.

At dawn, [I], personally leading the assembly of monks, chanted the *Renwang Huguo Jing* twenty-four times, praying for the pacification of the miasma of rebellion so as to prolong the dynastic mandate.

I humbly reflect that, dwelling as we do in a perilous pit, who can provide aid to escape this danger? When calamity has reached the stage of the solid ice, how can the power of spring be summoned to turn it back?
Looking upward, I implore the Great Awakened One; looking downward, I rely upon Your vast compassion. I earnestly consider that I, [Name], was born...
I have personally cast my lot in the dusty world while taking refuge in the Gate of Emptiness. Eating wood and wearing grass, even a drop of water has been moistened by the Sage’s grace;

dwelling in crags and caves, every inch of earth is sheltered by the Heavenly bounty. It would be difficult to repay such kindness even by sacrificing head and limb, and I can only offer a mere speck of dust in gratitude.

Yet, how could I have expected that during the height of the day, we would suddenly encounter the calamity of an eclipse? Famine has arrived in succession, and both the old and the young are [perishing].
The land has been turned into ravines and gullies; as arms have been raised in conflict time and again, half of the scholars and farmers have fled to the stagnant waters of the countryside.

The waves of the "whale" have not yet subsided south of the sea, while the iron-hoofed steeds remain arrogant north of the passes. The Central Plains are in a state of ruin and upheaval; the clouds of battle darken the sky as the blood of war stains them yellow.
The entire state of Chu was submerged, its original grass withered, and its bones turned white; once the Passes of Qin were breached, the soldiers threw down their blades and fled like rats.

When the defenses of Jin were also overrun, officials received the imperial edicts and bowed like blades of grass. Calamity was about to reach the ancestral altars, and the situation was inevitably pressing upon the Divine Capital.
Recently, because communications between the north and south have been severed, the anxiety of those above and below has become particularly acute. [The] monks...
My robes being frail, I merely harbor the sincerity of one offering his back to the sun; yet the Buddha’s virtue may be relied upon to reverently proclaim the scriptures for protecting the state.

I humbly pray that the Golden Wheel may forever stabilize the world and the Great Tortoise-Pole remain eternally at peace; that the clash of blades and spears be instantly extinguished, and the groans of distress throughout the four quarters suddenly cease.

The rebel troops have fled far away, and the exhaustion of the myriad people has been entirely relieved. As sun and moon alternate in their brilliance, they hang perpetually over the boundless reaches;
as earth and heaven interact in harmony, they together brew the auspiciousness of Great Peace. Throughout the land, there are records of great abundance;
throughout the heavens, the signs of a peaceful age are suspended. (I), [Name], cannot restrain my utmost sincerity in this fervent supplication.
